title: Reply to "Comment on 'Topography of Fermi arcs in t-PtBi2 using high-resolution angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy'"
summary: In a recent work [1] we demonstrated that the Fermi arcs in t-PtBi2 are indeed disconnected segments of the Fermi surface. We showed that the surface state band crosses EF between Weyl points and is has finite band gap at all other momenta until it merges with bulk bands. We did not find evidence of a superconducting gap in the spectra down to 3K. In recent Comment, Sergey Borisenko reanalyzed data from repository posted with our paper and concluded that a superconducting gap with i-wave symmetry is present in our data up to temperatures of 19K. We argue that this claim arises from incorrect identification of the location of Fermi arc and confusion between band gap and superconducting gap. This error was compounded by the fact that Author of the Comment analyzed data from interpolated images used for mapping the Fermi surface that are not suitable for extraction of energy gap on meV scale. This fact was previously communicated to the Author of the Comment during e-mail exchange. We maintain that our conclusion of absence of a superconducting gap above 3 K are valid and consistent with recent STM measurements performed on the same samples, which found surface superconductivity with Tc = 3K, below the temperature at which the data for our ARPES paper was measured.

AI.tldr: This is a Reply to a Comment. The authors defend their ARPES conclusion that t-PtBi2 shows no superconducting gap above 3 K, arguing that the Comment's claimed i-wave gap (up to 19 K) stems from misidentifying the Fermi arc location, confusing a band gap with a superconducting gap, and analyzing interpolated images unsuitable for meV-scale gap extraction.
AI.motivation: Borisenko's Comment reanalyzed the authors' deposited data and claimed a superconducting gap with i-wave symmetry persists up to 19 K, directly contradicting the original paper's finding of no gap above 3 K. The authors must rebut this to uphold the validity of their ARPES results and their interpretation of the Fermi arcs and surface band structure in t-PtBi2.
AI.method: Reexamination and argumentation on the original ARPES data and methodology: the authors identify the Comment's errors as (i) incorrect identification of the Fermi arc location, (ii) confusion between a band gap and a superconducting gap, and (iii) use of interpolated images created for Fermi-surface mapping, which cannot resolve gaps on the meV scale; they note this limitation was previously communicated to the Comment's author by e-mail.
AI.result: The Comment's claimed superconducting gap (i-wave, up to 19 K) is attributed to misinterpretation and inappropriate data usage rather than a genuine spectral feature. The original conclusions—disconnected Fermi arc segments, surface band crossing the Fermi level between Weyl nodes with a finite gap elsewhere until merging with bulk bands, and absence of a superconducting gap down to 3 K—are maintained and corroborated by recent STM measurements on the same samples showing surface superconductivity with Tc = 3 K.
AI.conclusion: The authors' finding of no superconducting gap above 3 K in t-PtBi2 is valid. The Comment's i-wave-gap claim is rejected as an artifact of data misinterpretation, and consistency with STM results (Tc = 3 K, below the ARPES measurement temperature) reinforces the original work.

title: Sideband fingerprint of the Leggett mode in terahertz two-dimensional coherent spectroscopy of multiband superconductors
summary: Collective modes of the superconducting condensate encode fundamental information on the pairing interaction, yet their direct detection remains experimentally challenging. In multiband superconductors, the Leggett mode, i.e., a coherent oscillation of the relative phase between two condensates, is Raman-active and couples to light only nonlinearly in ordinary situations. Here we show theoretically that terahertz two-dimensional coherent spectroscopy (2DCS) provides a direct fingerprint of the Leggett mode (with frequency $ω_L$) through sideband emission at the detection frequency $ω_t = ω_L\pmΩ$ ($Ω$ is the central frequency of the incident pulses) in the nonlinear 2D spectrum. The key insight is that the finite duration of the THz pulses is the physical mechanism that makes the mode accessible: the broad spectral content of a finite pulse provides the nonlinear frequency combinations needed to resonantly excite the mode at ωL without any prior knowledge of its value or tuning of external parameters. We demonstrate robustness of this signature against temperature and quasiparticle relaxation, and show that sweeping $Ω$ allows unambiguous identification of the Leggett mode.

AI.tldr: Terahertz 2D coherent spectroscopy can directly fingerprint the Leggett mode in multiband superconductors via sideband emission at ωt = ωL ± Ω, with the finite THz pulse duration enabling resonant excitation without prior knowledge of the mode frequency.
AI.motivation: The Leggett mode, a coherent oscillation of the relative phase between condensates in multiband superconductors, encodes fundamental pairing information but is Raman-active and couples to light only nonlinearly, making its direct detection experimentally challenging.
AI.method: A theoretical study employing terahertz two-dimensional coherent spectroscopy (2DCS), analyzing the nonlinear 2D spectrum for sideband emission at detection frequency ωt = ωL ± Ω, where Ω is the central frequency of the incident pulses. The mechanism relies on the broad spectral content of finite-duration THz pulses providing the nonlinear frequency combinations for resonant excitation.
AI.result: The Leggett mode (frequency ωL) produces a distinct sideband signature at ωt = ωL ± Ω in the nonlinear 2D spectrum. The signature is robust against temperature and quasiparticle relaxation, and sweeping Ω permits unambiguous identification of the mode.
AI.conclusion: THz 2DCS offers a direct, robust fingerprint of the Leggett mode, with finite pulse duration as the key enabling mechanism, allowing identification without prior knowledge of ωL or external parameter tuning.

title: Binary kagome superconducting candidates hosting topological electronic states
summary: Topological superconductivity has attracted broad interest because of its connection to Majorana fermions and quantum computation. Kagome materials provide a natural setting in which interesting electronic structures, topological surface states, and superconductivity may occur in nearby energy windows. Here we carry out a systematic first-principles search for binary kagome superconducting candidates with topological electronic states across several structural families $A_mB_n$ ($m$:$n$=3:1; 3:2; 1:1). The screening combines formation-energy and phonon-stability filtering, magnetic-ground-state searches, electron-phonon-coupling calculations, and topological electronic-structure analysis. We identify 286 nonmagnetic dynamically stable candidates for electron-phonon-coupling analysis, among which 84 have estimated transition temperatures above 3 K and seven exceed the $\sim 9$ K reference scale of existing ambient-pressure kagome superconductors. In addition, several systems are predicted to host abundant topological surface states near the Fermi level. NbBi is identified as a $\mathbb{Z}_2$ topological metal with clear Dirac-cone topological surface states and a kagome-derived flat band near $E_F$. Ti$_3$Si, with the largest estimated $T_\text{c}=15.2$ K in this dataset, shows nodal-line-derived drumhead surface states and selected nodes that survive spin-orbit coupling near $E_F$. Combining superconductivity with nontrivial topological electronic structures, the binary kagome compounds predicted here represent compact and chemically tunable candidate platforms for topological superconductivity and for exploring kagome-related quantum phenomena.

AI.tldr: A large-scale first-principles screen of binary kagome compounds identifies 286 dynamically stable nonmagnetic candidates, with 84 above 3 K and several combining superconductivity with topological surface states, notably NbBi and Ti3Si.
AI.motivation: Topological superconductivity is of broad interest due to its link to Majorana fermions and quantum computation. Kagome materials naturally combine interesting electronic structures, topological surface states, and superconductivity in nearby energy windows, motivating a systematic search for binary kagome superconducting candidates with topological electronic states.
AI.method: Systematic first-principles screening across several structural families AmBn (m:n = 3:1, 3:2, 1:1), combining formation-energy and phonon-stability filtering, magnetic-ground-state searches, electron-phonon-coupling calculations, and topological electronic-structure analysis.
AI.result: 286 nonmagnetic dynamically stable candidates were identified for electron-phonon-coupling analysis. 84 have estimated Tc above 3 K, and seven exceed the ~9 K reference scale of existing ambient-pressure kagome superconductors. Several systems are predicted to host abundant topological surface states near the Fermi level. NbBi is a Z2 topological metal with clear Dirac-cone topological surface states and a kagome-derived flat band near EF. Ti3Si, with the largest estimated Tc = 15.2 K in this dataset, shows nodal-line-derived drumhead surface states and selected nodes that survive spin-orbit coupling near EF.
AI.conclusion: Combining superconductivity with nontrivial topological electronic structures, the predicted binary kagome compounds represent compact and chemically tunable candidate platforms for topological superconductivity and for exploring kagome-related quantum phenomena.

title: Quantum critical superconductivity in a dense fermi dilute bose mixture close to mechanical instability
summary: We couple a metal to an uncondensed bose gas with repulsive bose-fermi interactions in two dimensions. Within the random phase approximation, we show that the density fluctuations of the bosons, which mediate the effective fermion-fermion attraction, become long ranged on appropriate tuning of interactions. This leads to parametrically enhanced superconducting temperatures $T_c \propto g$ as opposed to $T_c \propto \exp(-1/g)$ for the BCS case. The dilute bose gas density acts as the primary bottleneck to the enhancement. We discuss the conceptual difficulties of implementing this idea in electron-exciton mixtures.

AI.tldr: Coupling a metal to an uncondensed 2D repulsive Bose gas, the authors show (RPA) that boson density fluctuations mediating fermion attraction become long-ranged on tuning, yielding parametrically enhanced Tc ∝ g instead of BCS exp(-1/g).
AI.motivation: Standard BCS superconductivity suffers from an exponentially small Tc ∝ exp(-1/g), which severely limits achievable transition temperatures. The authors seek a mechanism to replace this exponential suppression with a power-law dependence on the coupling.
AI.method: They couple a metal to an uncondensed Bose gas with repulsive Bose-Fermi interactions in two dimensions and analyze the system within the random phase approximation (RPA), examining the density fluctuations of the bosons that mediate an effective fermion-fermion attraction.
AI.result: On appropriate tuning of interactions, the boson density fluctuations become long-ranged, leading to a parametrically enhanced superconducting temperature Tc ∝ g, in contrast to Tc ∝ exp(-1/g) for the BCS case. The dilute Bose gas density acts as the primary bottleneck to the enhancement.
AI.conclusion: The proposed mechanism offers a route to parametrically enhanced Tc via boson-mediated attraction, though limited by the dilute Bose gas density; the authors discuss the conceptual difficulties of implementing this idea in electron-exciton mixtures.

title: Breakdown of material-time scaling in the microscopic dynamics of metallic glasses
summary: Physical aging in glasses is often described using the concept of material time, which assumes the underlying relaxation mechanism to remain the same as in equilibrium, but with a rate that changes during aging. Whether material time also captures the microscopic dynamics of metallic glasses, which differ qualitatively between the glass and the equilibrium supercooled liquid, is unclear. Using simultaneous time-resolved X-ray diffraction and X-ray photon-correlation spectroscopy, we follow the full equilibration of a metallic glass after small temperature jumps starting from equilibrium. The time evolution of the first sharp diffraction peak position exhibits the asymmetry between temperature up- and down-jumps characteristic of material-time aging and is quantitatively described by the Tool-Narayanaswamy-Moynihan model, which is based on this concept. By contrast, the microscopic density-density autocorrelation functions strongly violate material-time scaling. Compressed-exponential relaxation emerges even after temperature changes as small as 4K, irrespective of the direction of the temperature jump, and continuously evolves into a stretched-exponential relaxation shape following the equilibration of the average structure. This behavior is consistent with a transient stress-mediated contribution associated with volumetric frustration that disappears upon equilibration. Our results show that a material time can describe the evolution of average structural properties even when the corresponding microscopic dynamics do not obey material-time scaling.

AI.tldr: Material-time scaling describes the evolution of average structural properties in a metallic glass after small temperature jumps, but the microscopic density-density dynamics violate this scaling, showing compressed-exponential relaxation that only becomes stretched-exponential upon equilibration.
AI.motivation: Material time is a common framework for physical aging, but its validity for metallic glasses is unclear because their microscopic dynamics differ qualitatively between the glass and the equilibrium supercooled liquid. The authors test whether material time captures the microscopic dynamics, not just average structural evolution, during full equilibration.
AI.method: Simultaneous time-resolved X-ray diffraction and X-ray photon-correlation spectroscopy (XPCS) track the equilibration of a metallic glass after small temperature jumps from equilibrium, probing both the first sharp diffraction peak (FSDP) position and density-density autocorrelation functions.
AI.result: The FSDP position shows the characteristic asymmetry between up- and down-jumps and is quantitatively reproduced by the Tool-Narayanaswamy-Moynihan (TNM) model. However, microscopic density-density autocorrelation functions strongly violate material-time scaling. Compressed-exponential relaxation appears even for temperature changes as small as 4 K, regardless of jump direction, and gradually becomes stretched-exponential as the average structure equilibrates. This is attributed to a transient stress-mediated contribution linked to volumetric frustration that vanishes upon equilibration.
AI.conclusion: Material time can describe the evolution of average structural properties even when the underlying microscopic dynamics do not obey material-time scaling, revealing a decoupling between average structural aging and microscopic relaxation in metallic glasses.

title: Structural crossover of complex networks: bridging degree correlation and fractality
summary: We investigate the relationship between long-range degree correlations and fractality in scale-free random networks. By analyzing degree correlations in scale-free random networks at the percolation threshold, at which a giant component emerges, we derive the ball volume $\tildeν_k(l)$, defined as the average number of nodes within distance $l$ from a root node with degree $k$. The resulting expression predicts a degree-dependent structural crossover. For $l\ll k^{1/(\df-1)}$, the ball volume grows as $\tildeν_k(l)\sim kl$, whereas for $l\gg k^{1/(\df-1)}$, it crosses over to the global fractal scaling $\tildeν_k(l)\sim l^{\df}$. Here, $\df$ is the fractal dimension of critical scale-free random networks. We further show that the structural crossover can be naturally understood in terms of critical branching processes and is also observed in empirical fractal networks.

AI.tldr: This paper links long-range degree correlations to fractality in scale-free random networks by deriving the ball volume at the percolation threshold, revealing a degree-dependent structural crossover between linear and fractal growth regimes, explained via critical branching processes and confirmed in empirical networks.
AI.motivation: The relationship between long-range degree correlations and fractality in scale-free random networks is not well understood. Understanding how degree correlations influence fractal scaling—particularly near the percolation threshold where a giant component emerges—could clarify the structural organization of complex networks.
AI.method: The authors analyze degree correlations in scale-free random networks at the percolation threshold. They derive the ball volume ν̃_k(l), the average number of nodes within distance l from a root node of degree k, and interpret the results using critical branching processes. They also test the predictions against empirical fractal networks.
AI.result: The derived expression predicts a degree-dependent structural crossover: for l ≪ k^{1/(d_f−1)}, the ball volume grows linearly as ν̃_k(l) ∼ kl, while for l ≫ k^{1/(d_f−1)}, it crosses over to global fractal scaling ν̃_k(l) ∼ l^{d_f}, where d_f is the fractal dimension of critical scale-free random networks.
AI.conclusion: The structural crossover is naturally explained by critical branching processes and is also observed in empirical fractal networks, supporting the link between long-range degree correlations and fractality.

title: Projective symmetry group classification of fermionic $Z_2$ spin liquids on the dipolar-octupolar pyrochlore magnets
summary: We construct and classify $Z_2$ quantum spin liquids (QSLs) of fermionic partons on the dipolar-octupolar (DO) pyrochlore lattice. The DO pseudospin shares the space-group and time-reversal algebra of the effective spin-1/2 Kramers doublet, its projective symmetry group (PSG) yields the same 48 symmetric $Z_2$ classes as the generic fermionic classification. We show, the distinct DO symmetry action, encoded in a set of sublattice-independent operators, selects a physically different set of symmetry-allowed mean-field channels, so that the resulting ansatze, spinon spectra, and observables differ from both the effective spin-1/2 case and the bosonic DO classification. Decomposing the anisotropic XYZ exchange model into all symmetric singlet and triplet hopping and pairing channels and minimizing the mean-field energy self-consistently, we obtain phase diagrams in the ($\tilde{J_x}, \tilde{J_z}$) plane in which only a few $Z_2$ states, several supporting gapless or flat-band spinon spectra, are stabilized. For these states we compute the spinon band structures, the low-temperature specific heat, and the dynamical spin structure factor, and we argue that the power-law specific-heat exponent is a diagnostic of the spinon nodal structure. A near-linear-in-temperature specific heat together with broad continua in the structure factor gives a fermionic-parton account of the gapless, fractionalized thermodynamics reported in DO materials such as $Nd_2ScNbO_7$, complementing the bosonic quantum-spin-ice picture of the Ce-based compounds. The work extends the fermionic-parton classification of DO pyrochlore QSLs beyond the $U(1)$ sector, where $Z_2$ topological order is realized equally naturally by fermionic and bosonic spinons.

AI.tldr: This work constructs and classifies Z2 quantum spin liquids of fermionic partons on the dipolar-octupolar pyrochlore lattice, obtaining self-consistent phase diagrams and identifying a power-law specific-heat exponent as a diagnostic of spinon nodal structure.
AI.motivation: The dipolar-octupolar (DO) pyrochlore lattice hosts effective spin-1/2 Kramers doublets with distinct symmetry actions, and prior classifications were limited to the U(1) sector or to bosonic partons. A fermionic-parton Z2 classification was lacking, motivating an extension beyond the U(1) sector to capture Z2 topological order on equal footing with bosonic spinons.
AI.method: The authors use projective symmetry group (PSG) analysis for fermionic partons on the DO pyrochlore lattice, obtaining 48 symmetric Z2 classes matching the generic fermionic classification but with a distinct DO symmetry action encoded in sublattice-independent operators. They decompose the anisotropic XYZ exchange model into all symmetric singlet and triplet hopping and pairing channels and minimize the mean-field energy self-consistently.
AI.result: The distinct DO symmetry action selects a physically different set of symmetry-allowed mean-field channels, yielding ansatze, spinon spectra, and observables that differ from both the effective spin-1/2 case and the bosonic DO classification. Phase diagrams in the (Jx, Jz) plane stabilize only a few Z2 states, several with gapless or flat-band spinon spectra. Computed spinon band structures, low-temperature specific heat, and dynamical spin structure factor reveal a power-law specific-heat exponent diagnostic of spinon nodal structure.
AI.conclusion: A near-linear-in-temperature specific heat together with broad continua in the structure factor provides a fermionic-parton account of the gapless, fractionalized thermodynamics reported in DO materials such as Nd2ScNbO7, complementing the bosonic quantum-spin-ice picture of Ce-based compounds. This extends the fermionic-parton classification of DO pyrochlore QSLs beyond the U(1) sector, where Z2 topological order is realized equally naturally by fermionic and bosonic spinons.

title: Thickness-Controlled Ferroelectric-to-Ionic Transport in CuCrP2S6 at Room Temperature
comment: Supplementary Material is included with the main manuscript. The main manuscript includes 6 figures
summary: Ambient-temperature coexistence of ferroelectricity, photoconductivity, and ionic transport in ultra-thin van der Waals (vdW) compound CuCrP2S6 (CCPS) offers significant potential for multifunctional electronic, photonic, and neuromorphic applications. However, ferroelectricity and ionic transport can become antagonistic when sharing a common atomic origin, like the copper ions in CCPS. We address this fundamental dichotomy by systematically investigating the thickness-dependent evolution of ferroelectricity, ionic migration, and memristive behavior in CCPS diodes via electrostatic and photo-assisted interfacial band tuning. Using piezoresponse, Kelvin probe, and conductive atomic force microscopy, alongside photoexcited transport measurements, we identify distinct thickness regimes. CCPS flakes thinner than ~ 40 nm exhibit robust, reversible ferroelectric (FE) switching. Conversely, thicker samples display suppressed switchable polarization, with electrical conduction dominated by Cu+ migration, filamentary memristive switching, and rectification reversal. Optical illumination further enhances ionic mobility via photogenerated carriers, driving photo-assisted ionic transport in non-FE flakes and a coupled photoferroionic response in FE flakes. These findings clarify how ferroelectricity fundamentally alters ionic transport dynamics in vdW ferroionic systems.

AI.tldr: Thickness governs whether CuCrP2S6 diodes are ferroelectric or ionically memristive: thin flakes (<~40 nm) show reversible ferroelectric switching, while thicker flakes are dominated by Cu+ migration, filamentary switching, and rectification reversal, with light coupling both behaviors.
AI.motivation: CuCrP2S6 (CCPS) combines ferroelectricity, photoconductivity, and ionic transport at room temperature, promising for multifunctional electronic, photonic, and neuromorphic devices. However, ferroelectricity and ionic transport may be antagonistic when they share a common atomic origin (Cu ions). This fundamental dichotomy is addressed through thickness-dependent study.
AI.method: Thickness-dependent investigation of ferroelectricity, ionic migration, and memristive behavior in CCPS diodes via electrostatic and photo-assisted interfacial band tuning. Characterization used piezoresponse force microscopy, Kelvin probe microscopy, conductive atomic force microscopy, and photoexcited transport measurements.
AI.result: Distinct thickness regimes identified: flakes thinner than ~40 nm show robust, reversible ferroelectric (FE) switching; thicker samples show suppressed switchable polarization, with conduction dominated by Cu+ migration, filamentary memristive switching, and rectification reversal. Optical illumination enhances ionic mobility via photogenerated carriers, driving photo-assisted ionic transport in non-FE flakes and a coupled photoferroionic response in FE flakes.
AI.conclusion: Thickness provides a control knob to switch between ferroelectric and ion-transport-dominated regimes in vdW ferroionic CCPS. Ferroelectricity fundamentally alters ionic transport dynamics in vdW ferroionic systems, and light enables coupled photoferroionic functionality relevant to multifunctional and neuromorphic applications.

title: Fluctuation-induced magnetoresistance in graphene Hall bars at charge neutrality
summary: In the temperature interval $T\sim 50 - 100 K$, the rate of electron-electron collisions in graphene devices may exceed the momentum relaxation rate due to disorder and electron-phonon scattering. In this regime, the motion of the electron liquid may be described by the hydrodynamic equations. In the hydrodynamic approximation, at the charge neutrality point the electric current is decoupled from the hydrodynamic flow, and the conductivity of the system is equal to the intrinsic conductivity of the electron liquid, $σ_0$. It was recently shown that the coupling of charge transport and hydrodynamic flow induced by the thermal fluctuations enhances the macroscopic conductivity of the system and results in very strong positive magnetoresistance (MR) at relatively weak fields. Here we develop a quantitative theory of the fluctuation mechanism of MR at charge neutrality and obtain analytic expressions for MR in graphene Hall bars. The functional dependence of MR on the magnetic field $H$ is sensitive to the Hall bar geometry and orientation relative to the current. We also account for the effect of momentum relaxation on MR.

AI.tldr: The paper develops a quantitative theory of fluctuation-induced magnetoresistance (MR) in graphene at charge neutrality, where electron transport is hydrodynamic. It derives analytic expressions for MR in Hall bars, showing geometric and orientation dependence, and includes momentum relaxation effects.
AI.motivation: At T ~ 50–100 K in graphene, electron-electron collisions dominate over momentum relaxation, enabling hydrodynamic electron liquid behavior. At the charge neutrality point, current decouples from hydrodynamic flow and conductivity equals the intrinsic value σ₀. Recent work showed thermal fluctuations couple charge transport and flow, enhancing macroscopic conductivity and producing strong positive MR at weak fields. However, a quantitative theory was lacking.
AI.method: The authors develop an analytical (quantitative) theory of the fluctuation mechanism of magnetoresistance at charge neutrality. They derive analytic expressions for MR in graphene Hall bars, accounting for the Hall bar geometry and its orientation relative to the current, and incorporate the effect of momentum relaxation.
AI.result: The theory yields analytic expressions for MR in Hall bars. The functional dependence of MR on magnetic field H is sensitive to Hall bar geometry and orientation relative to the current. Momentum relaxation is shown to affect the MR.
AI.conclusion: A quantitative theory of fluctuation-induced MR at charge neutrality in graphene is established, with geometry- and orientation-dependent analytic results, providing a framework to interpret experiments on hydrodynamic electron transport in graphene Hall bars.

title: RxnOptBench: Benchmarking LLMs for Reaction-Condition Optimization in Organic Methodology
summary: Chemical reaction-condition optimization -- choosing the catalyst, ligand, solvent, reagent, temperature, time, and atmosphere that jointly maximize yield and stereoselectivity -- is a central, judgement-laden subtask of organic methodology research that large language models are increasingly expected to support. Yet existing chemistry benchmarks evaluate reaction-class labelling, retrosynthesis, or SMILES manipulation, and do not ask models to read a real condition-screening table and pick the best set. We introduce RxnOptBench, a benchmark whose every option and precedent is a real wet-lab entry mined from the optimization tables of organic-methodology papers published in 2025, graded by a continuous relative score derived from a declared headline utility that combines reported yield with enantiomeric excess (ee), diastereomeric ratio (dr), and regioisomeric ratio (rr), and equipped with a paired precedents-vs-no-precedents design that isolates in-context use of literature evidence from parametric memorization. Across nine frontier LLMs and three Chemistry LLMs, even the best models leave substantial headroom: chemistry-specialized models fall to the random-baseline floor on multi-axis selection, while open-weight models have closed most of the gap to proprietary frontier models. We release the final human-reviewed benchmark test set and evaluation code.

AI.tldr: RxnOptBench is a new benchmark for chemical reaction-condition optimization built entirely from real 2025 wet-lab optimization tables, scored by a continuous utility combining yield, ee, dr, and rr, with a paired precedents-vs-no-precedents design; frontier and chemistry LLMs still show large headroom, with chemistry models collapsing to random on multi-axis selection.
AI.motivation: Reaction-condition optimization (selecting catalyst, ligand, solvent, reagent, temperature, time, atmosphere to jointly maximize yield and stereoselectivity) is a judgement-laden core task of organic methodology, yet existing chemistry benchmarks only test reaction-class labelling, retrosynthesis, or SMILES manipulation. No benchmark asks models to read a real condition-screening table and select the best set. Additionally, there is a need to disentangle genuine in-context use of literature evidence from parametric memorization.
AI.method: The authors introduce RxnOptBench. Every option and precedent is a real wet-lab entry mined from the optimization tables of organic-methodology papers published in 2025. Grading uses a continuous relative score derived from a declared headline utility that combines reported yield with enantiomeric excess (ee), diastereomeric ratio (dr), and regioisomeric ratio (rr). The benchmark features a paired precedents-vs-no-precedents design to isolate in-context use of literature evidence from parametric memorization. It is evaluated across nine frontier LLMs and three Chemistry LLMs, and the final human-reviewed test set and evaluation code are released.
AI.result: Even the best models leave substantial headroom. Chemistry-specialized models fall to the random-baseline floor on multi-axis selection, whereas open-weight models have closed most of the gap to proprietary frontier models.
AI.conclusion: RxnOptBench establishes reaction-condition optimization as a distinct, literature-grounded evaluation target and shows current LLMs, including chemistry-specialized ones, remain far from saturating it. The released human-reviewed test set and evaluation code provide a basis for measuring progress on multi-axis condition selection.

title: Developing Multi-Dimensional, Sequential sWeighting Routines for Reaction Selection with Emphasis on Kaon Identification at CLAS12
summary: In nuclear and particle physics experiments, event selection is often a multidimensional classification problem which involves several correlated observables. The widely used sWeight technique provides a statistically rigorous means of separating signal and background using discriminating variables, but its conventional formulation is generally applied to a single discriminating variable or a simultaneous multidimensional fit. In this paper we present a novel extension of the widely used sWeight technique, in which an arbitrary number of discriminating variables can be used to construct a multidimensional sequential framework. This method allows the extraction of signal distributions in controlled variables in a rigorous way. Particular attention is given to the treatment of signal and background correlations, as well as the propagation of statistical uncertainties through successive weighting stages. The method yields high-purity signal samples even in the presence of large and correlated backgrounds. As a benchmark application, the validity of this technique is demonstrated on kaon identification in a dataset collected with the CLAS12 detector at the Thomas Jefferson National Laboratory for cascade baryon searches. The final workflow is shown to be robust and consistent across different run periods and beam/detector conditions, demonstrating minimal systematical uncertainties associated with the method. Statistical uncertainties are proved to be evaluable using a bootstrap-based procedure. The method provides a general framework for multidimensional event weighting and is intended for application in complex analyses requiring robust signal selection in the presence of complex correlated backgrounds.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a multidimensional sequential generalization of the sWeight technique, using an arbitrary number of correlated discriminating variables to extract high-purity signal distributions, validated on kaon identification in CLAS12 cascade baryon searches.
AI.motivation: Event selection in nuclear and particle physics is a multidimensional classification problem with correlated observables. Conventional sWeight techniques are limited to a single discriminating variable or require a simultaneous multidimensional fit, restricting rigorous signal extraction in complex, correlated-background scenarios.
AI.method: The authors extend the sWeight technique into a multidimensional sequential framework, in which an arbitrary number of discriminating variables are applied through successive weighting stages. The method explicitly handles signal and background correlations and propagates statistical uncertainties across stages. Validation is performed via a benchmark on kaon identification using CLAS12 data for cascade baryon searches, with a bootstrap-based procedure for statistical uncertainty evaluation.
AI.result: The method yields high-purity signal samples even with large and correlated backgrounds. The final workflow is robust and consistent across different run periods and beam/detector conditions, with minimal systematic uncertainties. Statistical uncertainties are shown to be evaluable using a bootstrap-based procedure.
AI.conclusion: The proposed sequential multidimensional weighting provides a general framework for multidimensional event weighting, suitable for complex analyses requiring robust signal selection in the presence of complex correlated backgrounds.

title: AI-Assisted GPU optimization of the Stochastic Variational Method for Few-Body Boson System
summary: The stochastic variational method (SVM) is one of the most powerful methods to solve quantum few-body systems precisely in various fields, such as nuclear and atomic physics. To the best of our knowledge, no SVM code optimized for GPUs has been reported. We developed a parallel SVM code for few-body clusters of $^4$He atoms and optimized it for two GPU architectures, NVIDIA GH200 and AMD Instinct MI300A, with the entire code written by an AI coding agent. On the algorithmic side, we introduce the secular-equation method with the Gu--Eisenstat prescription for solving the generalized eigenvalue problem within the SVM framework. The main part of the code tuning is to batch the many small matrices so that the GPUs are used efficiently, together with an array layout in memory optimized for coalesced addressing. For the five-body system with 4800 SVM basis states, the tuned SVM code runs 16.2 (14.7) times faster on the NVIDIA GH200 (AMD MI300A) than the same tuned code on the Intel Xeon Max CPU system, and 168 (153) times faster than the first working CPU implementation. The achieved performance brings 6-body and larger cluster systems within reach.

AI.tldr: The authors developed the first GPU-optimized stochastic variational method (SVM) code for few-body $^4$He clusters, entirely written by an AI coding agent, achieving up to 168x speedup over the initial CPU version and enabling 6-body systems.
AI.motivation: SVM is a powerful tool for precisely solving quantum few-body systems (nuclear/atomic physics), but no GPU-optimized SVM code had been reported, leaving significant computational potential untapped.
AI.method: They wrote a parallel SVM code for $^4$He few-body clusters using an AI coding agent and optimized it for NVIDIA GH200 and AMD Instinct MI300A. Algorithmically, they introduced the secular-equation method with the Gu–Eisenstat prescription to solve the generalized eigenvalue problem. Code tuning centered on batching many small matrices for efficient GPU use and an array layout optimized for coalesced memory addressing.
AI.result: For a five-body system with 4800 SVM basis states, the tuned code ran 16.2x (NVIDIA GH200) and 14.7x (AMD MI300A) faster than the same tuned code on an Intel Xeon Max CPU system, and 168x (153x) faster than the first working CPU implementation.
AI.conclusion: GPU optimization of SVM yields dramatic performance gains, bringing 6-body and larger cluster systems within computational reach.

title: Interaction-induced period shift of the Kohn oscillation in a parity-time-symmetric harmonic trap
summary: The center of mass of a Bose--Einstein condensate in a harmonic trap oscillates at the trap frequency independently of the interactions. Without interactions a parity-time-symmetric gain-loss gradient leaves this frequency unchanged, and a cloud of the ground-state width is translated rigidly while the atom number is periodically modulated. With interactions the protection is lost, because the gain and the loss change the number of atoms; the modulated atom number drives the width of the cloud, and the width acts back on the center of mass. At small gain the period grows quadratically with the gain strength, with a coefficient that in the Thomas--Fermi regime is set by the size of the cloud alone. The family of periodic orbits continued from the Kohn oscillation can be followed up to a critical gain, where it comes into resonance with highly excited states of the trap, and over the computed families this critical gain decreases with the amplitude of the oscillation and with the size of the cloud. A five-variable moment model reproduces the period and the width of the cloud along the orbits nearly up to the critical gain.

AI.tldr: The Kohn oscillation of a Bose-Einstein condensate is protected against a parity-time-symmetric gain-loss gradient only in the non-interacting case; interactions break this protection and cause the oscillation period to grow quadratically with gain, up to a critical gain where the orbit resonates with trap excited states.
AI.motivation: The center-of-mass oscillation of a harmonically trapped Bose-Einstein condensate (Kohn mode) is famously independent of interactions. The authors ask whether this protection survives when a parity-time-symmetric gain-loss gradient is added, and how interactions modify the dynamics.
AI.method: Analysis of the center-of-mass and width dynamics under a parity-time-symmetric gain-loss gradient, including a reduced five-variable moment model, continuation of periodic orbits from the Kohn oscillation, and comparison with the Thomas-Fermi regime.
AI.result: Without interactions the oscillation frequency is unchanged and the ground-state-width cloud is translated rigidly with a periodically modulated atom number. With interactions the protection is lost: the modulated atom number drives the width, which feeds back on the center of mass. At small gain the period grows quadratically with gain strength, with a Thomas-Fermi coefficient set by the cloud size alone. Periodic orbits can be continued up to a critical gain where they resonate with highly excited trap states; this critical gain decreases with oscillation amplitude and cloud size. The five-variable moment model reproduces the period and width nearly up to the critical gain.
AI.conclusion: Interaction-induced coupling between atom number, cloud width, and center of mass destroys the Kohn-mode protection in a parity-time-symmetric gain-loss gradient. The resulting periodic orbits persist up to a critical gain determined by resonance with excited trap states, and a five-variable moment model captures the behavior nearly up to this threshold.

title: Lithium Niobate Surface-Acoustic-Wave Resonator for Very-High-Frequency Isolated Power Conversion
summary: Piezoelectric devices offer a promising magnetic-free alternative for high-frequency power electronics, enabling compact energy transfer with inherent galvanic isolation. Here we demonstrate a lithium niobate surface acoustic wave (SAW) resonator that enables isolated power transfer and addresses the challenges in existing piezoelectric devices for power applications, including operation frequencies, power delivery figure of merit (FOM), power handling, and electrical isolation. Our application-optimized 40-MHz SAW resonator, with the two electrically isolated interdigital transducers (IDTs) and acoustic Bragg mirrors, achieves a 25.7 W output power at a less than 15 °C temperature rise with only passive cooling through the back mounting side, and an isolation voltage of 2.17 kV. In DC-AC power conversion, we demonstrate a peak efficiency of 93.8 %, a power delivery FOM of 13.47 mW/V$^2$ and a peak chip power density of 81.7 W/cm$^3$. DC-DC conversion is also demonstrated by connecting a diode rectifier to the output IDT, despite efficiency degrading to 52.7 %. Our results advance SAW devices as one of the core components for next-generation very-high-frequency, miniaturized, high-density, magnetic-free, isolated power converters.

AI.tldr: A 40-MHz lithium niobate SAW resonator with isolated IDTs and acoustic Bragg mirrors enables magnetic-free isolated power transfer, delivering 25.7 W at <15 °C rise, 2.17 kV isolation, and 93.8 % peak DC-AC efficiency.
AI.motivation: Piezoelectric devices are a promising magnetic-free alternative for high-frequency power electronics, offering compact energy transfer with inherent galvanic isolation. However, existing piezoelectric devices face challenges for power applications, including limited operation frequencies, low power delivery figure of merit (FOM), insufficient power handling, and inadequate electrical isolation.
AI.method: The authors designed an application-optimized 40-MHz lithium niobate surface acoustic wave (SAW) resonator featuring two electrically isolated interdigital transducers (IDTs) and acoustic Bragg mirrors. They evaluated it for power transfer, DC-AC conversion, and DC-DC conversion (via a diode rectifier connected to the output IDT).
AI.result: The device achieves 25.7 W output power with less than 15 °C temperature rise under passive back-side cooling, an isolation voltage of 2.17 kV, a peak DC-AC efficiency of 93.8 %, a power delivery FOM of 13.47 mW/V², and a peak chip power density of 81.7 W/cm³. DC-DC conversion was demonstrated but with efficiency degrading to 52.7 %.
AI.conclusion: These results position SAW devices as core components for next-generation very-high-frequency, miniaturized, high-density, magnetic-free, isolated power converters.

title: Layer-Asymmetry-Induced Topological Superconductivity in High-T$_c$ Bilayer Nickelates
summary: The recent discovery of high-T$_c$ superconductivity in bilayer nickelates has highlighted the crucial role of interlayer coupling and motivated proposals for dominant interlayer pairing. Whether such pairing can support topological superconductivity, however, remains unexplored. Here, we demonstrate that substrate-supported bilayer nickelate thin films can host an intrinsic time-reversal-invariant topological superconducting phase protected by diagonal mirror symmetry. Using a two-orbital model derived from first-principles calculations, we show that a modest layer-asymmetric potential and layer-staggered Rashba spin-orbit coupling drive the system into this topological phase over a broad parameter range with a dominant interlayer pairing. The nontrivial topology arises from a reversal of the pairing sign on one of the spin-split bonding Fermi surfaces and is characterized by a nonzero mirror winding number along the diagonal direction, as well as a Majorana Kramers pair at the [11] edge. The phase also features bulk gap nodes located slightly away from the diagonal directions, featuring chiral charge and zero-energy flat bands. We discuss experimental routes for realizing and tuning this phase. Our results establish high-T$_c$ bilayer nickelates as a promising platform for topological superconductivity, where tunable topological transitions and Majorana boundary modes can provide probes of unconventional pairing.

AI.tldr: Substrate-supported bilayer nickelate thin films can host an intrinsic time-reversal-invariant topological superconducting phase, protected by diagonal mirror symmetry, arising from dominant interlayer pairing in a two-orbital model.
AI.motivation: The discovery of high-Tc superconductivity in bilayer nickelates highlights interlayer coupling and motivates proposals for dominant interlayer pairing, but whether such pairing can support topological superconductivity remains unexplored.
AI.method: A two-orbital model derived from first-principles calculations is used, incorporating a modest layer-asymmetric potential and layer-staggered Rashba spin-orbit coupling.
AI.result: A topological phase emerges over a broad parameter range with dominant interlayer pairing. Nontrivial topology stems from pairing-sign reversal on one spin-split bonding Fermi surface, characterized by a nonzero mirror winding number along the diagonal direction and a Majorana Kramers pair at the [11] edge. The phase also exhibits bulk gap nodes slightly off the diagonal directions, with chiral charge and zero-energy flat bands.
AI.conclusion: Bilayer nickelates are established as a promising platform for topological superconductivity, where tunable topological transitions and Majorana boundary modes can probe unconventional pairing; experimental realization and tuning routes are discussed.

title: Universal energy barrier for plastic flow in a network glass
summary: Shear transformations are the elementary events of plasticity in glasses and underpin many mesoscopic models of plastic flow, yet their atomic origin and energetics remain difficult to establish. Here we use a machine-learned interatomic potential to show that, in amorphous carbon as a representative network glass, a shear transformation corresponds to the breaking or formation of a single covalent bond. The simplicity of the associated reaction coordinate, the bond length, enables us to extract energy landscapes and barriers. Despite the intrinsic structural disorder, we find that all energy landscapes collapse onto a universal barrier shape. What remains bond-specific is a single scale, the bond-jump distance, which fixes the barrier height through a cubic law. Combined with the activation statistics of shear transformations, this yields a model that predicts the plastic flow stress from independently determined bond-level quantities. Our results provide microscopic support for phenomenological models of plastic flow in glasses and suggest a route towards a quantitative description of amorphous plasticity.

AI.tldr: Using a machine-learned interatomic potential in amorphous carbon, this work shows a shear transformation in network glasses reduces to breaking/forming a single covalent bond, whose universal energy-landscape shape and cubic bond-jump-distance law predict plastic flow stress from bond-level quantities.
AI.motivation: Shear transformations are the elementary events of plasticity in glasses and underlie many mesoscopic models of plastic flow, but their atomic origin and energetics have been difficult to establish.
AI.method: A machine-learned interatomic potential is used to simulate amorphous carbon as a representative network glass. The reaction coordinate is identified with the bond length, allowing extraction of energy landscapes and barriers for individual shear transformations, followed by analysis of their collapse and activation statistics.
AI.result: A shear transformation corresponds to the breaking or formation of a single covalent bond. Despite intrinsic structural disorder, all energy landscapes collapse onto a universal barrier shape; only the bond-jump distance remains bond-specific and sets the barrier height via a cubic law. Combined with activation statistics, this yields a model predicting plastic flow stress from independently determined bond-level quantities.
AI.conclusion: The results provide microscopic support for phenomenological models of plastic flow in glasses and suggest a route toward a quantitative description of amorphous plasticity.

title: Probing fluctuating hydrodynamics through current fluctuations in hard rod gas
summary: We study the full counting statistics of the integrated current in a one-dimensional hard-rod gas in equilibrium, employing two recently proposed fluctuating hydrodynamic frameworks: (i) Ballistic Macroscopic Fluctuation Theory (BMFT) and (ii) diffusive fluctuating hydrodynamic theory based on correlated Brownian motion approximation of hard-rod quasiparticles (CBFHD). We investigate how the predictions of these two approaches compare with each other and with the underlying microscopic dynamics. We show within BMFT that the current distribution admits a large-deviation form under ballistic scaling, and we derive an explicit expression for the large-deviation function, valid for an arbitrary inhomogeneous initial state factorized in point-particle coordinates. The corresponding current cumulants are also obtained. We subsequently analyze the current statistics within the CBFHD framework, which explicitly incorporates stochastic noise and dissipative terms, and demonstrate that the current distribution likewise obeys a large-deviation principle in this approach. We find that, while BMFT predictions for the first few cumulants and the rate function are in excellent agreement with direct numerical simulations of the microscopic hard-rod dynamics, CBFHD prediction is not. We further verify the predictions of the CBFHD independently using a collection of correlated Brownian motions, which provides an approximate description of the dynamics of hard-rod quasiparticles. Our findings indicate that CBFHD does not accurately capture large-scale current fluctuations in the hard-rod gas, whereas BMFT yields predictions in quantitative agreement with the microscopic dynamics, at least in the context of full counting statistics.

AI.tldr: Comparative study of current full counting statistics in a 1D hard-rod gas using Ballistic Macroscopic Fluctuation Theory (BMFT) versus correlated-Brownian-motion fluctuating hydrodynamics (CBFHD); BMFT matches microscopic simulations while CBFHD does not.
AI.motivation: Two recently proposed fluctuating hydrodynamic frameworks—BMFT and CBFHD—make competing predictions for current fluctuations in hard-rod gases, but their accuracy against the underlying microscopic dynamics had not been systematically benchmarked.
AI.method: Equilibrium full counting statistics of the integrated current in a 1D hard-rod gas. Within BMFT, derive the large-deviation form and explicit large-deviation function (plus current cumulants) under ballistic scaling for an arbitrary inhomogeneous initial state factorized in point-particle coordinates. Within CBFHD, incorporate stochastic noise and dissipative terms and derive its large-deviation principle. Validate CBFHD independently via a collection of correlated Brownian motions approximating hard-rod quasiparticle dynamics. Compare both against direct numerical simulations of microscopic hard-rod dynamics.
AI.result: BMFT predictions for the first few cumulants and the rate function agree excellently with microscopic simulations. CBFHD likewise obeys a large-deviation principle, but its cumulant and rate-function predictions disagree with the microscopic dynamics; the correlated-Brownian-motion construction confirms the CBFHD results internally.
AI.conclusion: CBFHD fails to capture large-scale current fluctuations in the hard-rod gas, whereas BMFT yields quantitatively accurate predictions for full counting statistics, at least in this setting.

title: Fractionalization-Induced Time-Reversal Symmetry Breaking at Continuous Superconducting Transitions in Low-Symmetry Kondo Lattices
summary: In conventional Landau theory, simultaneous continuous onset of superconductivity and the breaking of additional symmetries generally requires a multidimensional order parameter or fine tuning. We show that symmetry fractionalization provides a different route. In a Kondo lattice with a $\mathbb Z_2$ spin liquid, the Kondo fields inherit the projective symmetry action of the spinons. When the projective time-reversal action on these fields squares to $-1$, the projective symmetry algebra forbids a condensate that preserves time-reversal symmetry and enforces twofold degeneracy of the critical modes. Because Kondo condensation in a $\mathbb Z_2$ spin liquid also breaks electromagnetic $U(1)$ symmetry, superconductivity and time-reversal symmetry breaking can emerge at a single continuous transition, even if crystal symmetry admits only one-dimensional irreducible representations. We demonstrate this mechanism in an anisotropic Kondo-Kitaev model, where superconductivity and the breaking of time-reversal and mirror symmetries emerge simultaneously.

AI.tldr: Symmetry fractionalization in a $\mathbb Z_2$ spin liquid Kondo lattice enables superconductivity and time-reversal (plus mirror) symmetry breaking at a single continuous transition, even with only one-dimensional irreps.
AI.motivation: In conventional Landau theory, simultaneous continuous onset of superconductivity and breaking of additional symmetries generally requires a multidimensional order parameter or fine tuning. This work seeks an alternative, more generic route to such multi-symmetry-breaking continuous transitions.
AI.method: The authors analyze a Kondo lattice coupled to a $\mathbb Z_2$ spin liquid. The Kondo fields inherit the projective symmetry action of the spinons; when the projective time-reversal action squares to $-1$, the projective symmetry algebra forbids a time-reversal-preserving condensate and enforces twofold degeneracy of critical modes. The mechanism is demonstrated in an anisotropic Kondo-Kitaev model.
AI.result: Because Kondo condensation in a $\mathbb Z_2$ spin liquid also breaks electromagnetic $U(1)$ symmetry, superconductivity and time-reversal symmetry breaking emerge at a single continuous transition despite crystal symmetry admitting only one-dimensional irreps. In the anisotropic Kondo-Kitaev model, superconductivity and breaking of time-reversal and mirror symmetries occur simultaneously.
AI.conclusion: Symmetry fractionalization provides a distinct route to simultaneous continuous onset of superconductivity and additional symmetry breaking, circumventing the Landau requirement for multidimensional order parameters or fine tuning; this is realized in a Kondo-Kitaev model.

title: Distinguishing sodium-ion penetration and sustained transport in realistic hard carbon nanostructures
summary: Hard carbons are promising anodes for sodium-ion energy storage, yet the relationship between their heterogeneous microstructure and sodium transport remains poorly understood. Here, we combine machine-learning-generated hard-carbon structures with molecular dynamics simulations of explicit 1 M NaPF6 in ethylene carbonate/dimethyl carbonate electrolyte to investigate sodium storage and transport across carbon structures with densities from 0.5 to 2.0 g cm-3. Increasing carbon density produces less accessible pore networks and greater graphitic local ordering, allowing the influence of microstructure on electrochemical response and Na+ transport to be examined systematically. Sodium uptake increases with applied potential but decreases strongly with carbon density, while electrode charging persists even in the densest structure, where Na+ uptake remains very small. Coordination analysis shows increasing interaction with the carbon framework under applied potential, while Na+ retains a partially solvated environment. Three-dimensional trajectory analysis reveals heterogeneous, predominantly tortuous transport pathways, with the more open HC-C1 structure supporting broader penetration and greater sustained displacement. Maximum penetration depth and retained displacement are not equivalent: ions can transiently reach deep regions of denser carbon structures before returning towards the electrolyte interface. Potential-of-mean-force analysis further shows that deep penetration occurs across a range of projected free-energy changes and cannot be described by a single energetic criterion. These results show that Na+ storage and transport are governed by the interplay between electrostatic driving force, electrolyte solvation, pore accessibility and confinement, highlighting carbon microstructure as a key determinant of sustained ionic penetration.

AI.tldr: Combining machine-learning-generated hard-carbon structures with MD simulations of explicit electrolyte, this work systematically links carbon density (0.5–2.0 g cm⁻³) to Na⁺ storage and transport, showing that microstructure, solvation, and electrostatic driving force jointly govern sustained ionic penetration.
AI.motivation: Hard carbons are promising sodium-ion battery anodes, but the relationship between their heterogeneous microstructure and sodium transport/storage remains poorly understood. A systematic, atomistic understanding of how carbon microstructure controls Na⁺ behavior is needed.
AI.method: Machine-learning-generated hard-carbon structures were combined with molecular dynamics simulations of explicit 1 M NaPF6 in ethylene carbonate/dimethyl carbonate electrolyte. Carbon densities spanning 0.5–2.0 g cm⁻³ were examined, using sodium uptake, coordination analysis, three-dimensional trajectory analysis, and potential-of-mean-force calculations.
AI.result: Sodium uptake increases with applied potential but decreases strongly with carbon density; charging persists even in the densest structure with very small Na⁺ uptake. Na⁺ retains a partially solvated environment while interacting more with the carbon framework under potential. Transport is heterogeneous and predominantly tortuous, with the more open HC-C1 supporting broader penetration and greater sustained displacement. Maximum penetration depth and retained displacement are not equivalent, and deep penetration cannot be described by a single energetic criterion.
AI.conclusion: Na⁺ storage and transport are governed by the interplay between electrostatic driving force, electrolyte solvation, pore accessibility, and confinement, highlighting carbon microstructure as a key determinant of sustained ionic penetration.

title: Chiral Vacuum Engineering of Quantum Hall Matter
summary: We reveal that a chiral cavity distinguishes the resonant and antiresonant interactions between a two-dimensional electron gas and the cavity vacuum. For co-rotating helicities, the modes anticross, exhibiting vacuum Rabi splitting, and retain a bare vacuum ground state. For counter-rotating helicities, the modes cross, acquiring vacuum-mediated energy shifts and a two-mode squeezed ground state. We trace the origin of these observations to the SU(2) and SU(1,1) symmetries of the respective Hamiltonians and present their spectroscopic signatures in chiral photonic crystal cavities. We further predict that cavity chirality produces a handedness-dependent correction to Hall resistivity at finite polariton broadening, while such a correction is not present in an achiral cavity. For the longitudinal resistivity, we find an asymmetric response of the Shubnikov--de Haas oscillations for the different helicities. Finally, we present an experimentally accessible route for detecting the squeezed ground state through current fluctuations. Parameters based on a recently demonstrated terahertz chiral cavity place these effects within experimental reach.

AI.tldr: A chiral cavity differentiates resonant (anticrossing, bare vacuum) from antiresonant (crossing, squeezed ground state) light-matter interactions in a 2D electron gas, rooted in SU(2) vs SU(1,1) symmetries, and yields handedness-dependent corrections to Hall and Shubnikov-de Haas transport.
AI.motivation: Chiral (handed) cavities introduce a helicity degree of freedom absent in achiral cavities, yet how cavity chirality reshapes the resonant versus antiresonant coupling between a two-dimensional electron gas and the cavity vacuum, and what experimentally observable consequences follow, remains unexplored.
AI.method: The authors analyze the Hamiltonian describing a two-dimensional electron gas coupled to a chiral cavity vacuum, separating co-rotating and counter-rotating helicities. They identify the underlying SU(2) and SU(1,1) symmetries of the respective Hamiltonians, derive spectroscopic signatures in chiral photonic crystal cavities, and compute transport responses (Hall and longitudinal resistivity) at finite polariton broadening. A detection scheme via current fluctuations is proposed.
AI.result: For co-rotating helicities, modes anticross with vacuum Rabi splitting and retain a bare vacuum ground state. For counter-rotating helicities, modes cross, acquire vacuum-mediated energy shifts, and exhibit a two-mode squeezed ground state. Cavity chirality produces a handedness-dependent correction to Hall resistivity at finite polariton broadening (absent in achiral cavities), and an asymmetric Shubnikov-de Haas response in longitudinal resistivity for the two helicities.
AI.conclusion: Cavity chirality fundamentally distinguishes resonant and antiresonant vacuum interactions, with symmetry principles (SU(2), SU(1,1)) governing the physics. The predicted handedness-dependent transport corrections and squeezed-ground-state signatures are within experimental reach using a recently demonstrated terahertz chiral cavity, offering an accessible route to probe vacuum squeezing via current fluctuations.

title: libterachem.py: Modular development of electronic structure methods with graphical processing units
summary: We present libterachem.py, a Python interface and method framework that facilitates development and prototyping of electronic structure methods while leveraging TeraChem's optimized graphical processing unit (GPU) operations. Direct access to these building blocks and their intermediate quantities allows users to assemble and modify methods within Python while reusing the underlying GPU implementations. A layered architecture, programmable at both the operation level and the method level, supports numerical experimentation, composition of complete electronic structure methods with interchangeable components, and integration with external scientific libraries. We illustrate operation-level use with grid pruning for least-squares tensor hypercontraction and with exchange--correlation functionals supplied through LibXC and by the machine-learned Skala functional. We illustrate method-level use with dispersion corrections, periodic calculations, and geometry optimization with an external optimizer. Python-driven self-consistent-field calculations using libterachem.py incur no significant computational overhead compared to native TeraChem and preserve its multi-GPU scaling. A photoactive yellow protein QM/MM molecular dynamics application further demonstrates throughput comparable to native TeraChem in a workflow composed with external simulation libraries. These results establish libterachem.py as a platform for method development and interoperable molecular simulation that retains the performance of TeraChem's GPU operations.

AI.tldr: libterachem.py is a Python interface and method framework that enables prototyping and development of electronic structure methods by exposing TeraChem's optimized GPU operations at both the operation and method levels, with negligible overhead versus native TeraChem.
AI.motivation: Developing and prototyping new electronic structure methods typically requires either reimplementing high-performance GPU kernels or sacrificing performance for flexibility. There is a need for a platform that combines the accessibility of Python with the performance of optimized GPU-accelerated quantum chemistry operations, enabling experimentation and interoperability with external libraries.
AI.method: The authors build libterachem.py, a layered Python interface and method framework around TeraChem. It exposes GPU building blocks and their intermediate quantities for operation-level programming (e.g., grid pruning for least-squares tensor hypercontraction; exchange-correlation functionals via LibXC and the machine-learned Skala functional), and supports method-level composition of complete methods with interchangeable components (dispersion corrections, periodic calculations, geometry optimization with an external optimizer), plus integration with external scientific libraries.
AI.result: Python-driven self-consistent-field calculations using libterachem.py show no significant computational overhead compared to native TeraChem while preserving its multi-GPU scaling. A photoactive yellow protein QM/MM molecular dynamics application achieves throughput comparable to native TeraChem in a workflow composed with external simulation libraries.
AI.conclusion: libterachem.py establishes a platform for electronic structure method development and interoperable molecular simulation that retains the performance of TeraChem's GPU operations, enabling both operation-level and method-level experimentation without sacrificing efficiency.

title: Explainable Molecular Structure Inference from GC--MS with Diffusion Models and LLM Reranking
summary: GC--EI--MS is an important technique for analyzing volatile and semivolatile compounds in complex samples. However, conventional methods rely heavily on reference spectral library matching, limiting their ability to identify compounds absent from these libraries and to infer complete molecular structures directly from fragmentation information. Here, we present DiffGCMS, a spectrum-conditioned discrete graph diffusion model for de novo structure elucidation from GC--EI--MS, and further develop a framework that integrates DiffGCMS with second-stage reasoning by a large language model (LLM). In the first stage, DiffGCMS generates candidate molecular structures from input spectra; in the second stage, the LLM uses mass spectral information to validate, repair, and rerank the candidates and provides interpretable analysis of fragment-ion peaks. This framework can generate plausible molecular structures for compounds absent from reference spectral libraries and provide traceable evidence supporting its decisions. On a test set comprising 13,696 spectra from NIST 20, the generative model achieved Acc@1 and Acc@10 of 6.01\% and 15.76\%, respectively. On the test subset containing molecules with no more than 10 heavy atoms, LLM-assisted molecular graph repair and reranking increased Acc@1 from 21.28\% to 21.95\%, Acc@10 from 46.91\% to 47.99\%, and candidate validity from 91.04\% to 100\%. These results demonstrate that spectrum-aware postprocessing can correct errors produced by the generative model while providing auditable and traceable explanations for the final ranking.

AI.tldr: DiffGCMS is a spectrum-conditioned discrete graph diffusion model for de novo structure elucidation from GC-EI-MS, combined with LLM-based second-stage reasoning for candidate validation, repair, and reranking.
AI.motivation: Conventional GC-EI-MS analysis relies heavily on reference spectral library matching, which limits identification of compounds absent from libraries and prevents direct inference of complete molecular structures from fragmentation data.
AI.method: A two-stage framework: (1) DiffGCMS, a spectrum-conditioned discrete graph diffusion model, generates candidate molecular structures from input spectra; (2) an LLM performs second-stage reasoning using mass spectral information to validate, repair, and rerank candidates and provide interpretable fragment-ion peak analysis.
AI.result: On 13,696 NIST 20 spectra, the generative model achieved Acc@1 of 6.01% and Acc@10 of 15.76%. On the subset with molecules of no more than 10 heavy atoms, LLM-assisted graph repair and reranking raised Acc@1 from 21.28% to 21.95%, Acc@10 from 46.91% to 47.99%, and candidate validity from 91.04% to 100%.
AI.conclusion: Spectrum-aware postprocessing can correct generative model errors while providing auditable and traceable explanations for the final ranking, enabling plausible structure generation for compounds absent from reference libraries.

title: Experimental Bench Validation of a Computational Fluid-Structure Interaction Model of Transcatheter Aortic Valve Dynamics
summary:
Purpose: This study extends our fluid-structure interaction (FSI) framework for surgical bioprosthetic heart valves in an experimental pulse duplicator to a transcatheter aortic valve replacement (TAVR) device. We assess hemodynamic and leaflet kinematic agreement across pulse rates and the transferability of calibrated boundary-model parameters.
  Methods: We compared simulated and experimental pressure, volumetric flow rate, projected dynamic valve area (PDVA), and leaflet kinematics at 60, 70, and 80 beats per minute (bpm). Reduced-order boundary-model parameters were calibrated using only data acquired at 70 bpm and were subsequently held fixed. At each pulse rate, a condition-specific pump-pressure waveform was constructed from the measured upstream pressure and flow rate. The 60 and 80 bpm cases therefore evaluate parameter transfer under measurement-informed upstream forcing.
  Results: Across the three conditions, normalized root-mean-square errors are 2.88-3.08% for aortic flow rate, 7.64-8.07% for upstream ventricular pressure, 3.50-6.21% for downstream aortic pressure, and 3.07-4.70% for PDVA. The simulations reproduce the principal pressure, flow, valve-opening, and valve-closure features. The downstream aortic pressure and PDVA measurements at 60 and 80 bpm were not used to construct the upstream forcing or recalibrate the model parameters and therefore provide the principal out-of-calibration validation evidence.
  Conclusion: The results provide conditional experimental bench validation evidence for downstream hemodynamics and valve dynamics under measurement-informed upstream forcing and support boundary-parameter transfer across pulse rates without recalibration. This work advances an experimentally supported, high-fidelity FSI framework for evaluating TAVR device performance.

AI.tldr: The study validates an FSI framework for a TAVR device in a pulse duplicator, showing accurate hemodynamics and leaflet kinematics across 60–80 bpm with boundary-model parameters calibrated only at 70 bpm.
AI.motivation: To extend a previously developed FSI framework for surgical bioprosthetic heart valves to a transcatheter aortic valve replacement (TAVR) device, and to test whether calibrated reduced-order boundary-model parameters remain valid across different pulse rates without recalibration.
AI.method: Simulated and experimental pressure, volumetric flow rate, projected dynamic valve area (PDVA), and leaflet kinematics were compared at 60, 70, and 80 bpm. Reduced-order boundary-model parameters were calibrated using only 70 bpm data and then held fixed. For each pulse rate, a condition-specific pump-pressure waveform was constructed from measured upstream pressure and flow rate, making the 60 and 80 bpm cases tests of parameter transfer under measurement-informed upstream forcing.
AI.result: Normalized RMSEs across the three conditions were 2.88–3.08% for aortic flow rate, 7.64–8.07% for upstream ventricular pressure, 3.50–6.21% for downstream aortic pressure, and 3.07–4.70% for PDVA. Simulations reproduced the principal pressure, flow, valve-opening, and valve-closure features, with downstream aortic pressure and PDVA at 60 and 80 bpm serving as the main out-of-calibration validation evidence.
AI.conclusion: The results provide conditional experimental bench validation for downstream hemodynamics and valve dynamics under measurement-informed upstream forcing, and support transfer of boundary-model parameters across pulse rates without recalibration, advancing an experimentally supported high-fidelity FSI framework for evaluating TAVR device performance.

title: Floquet density response in laser-assisted fast-electron scattering from solids
summary: We extend the Bethe--Floquet formalism of Joachain and coworkers, originally developed for laser-assisted electron--atom collisions, to inelastic scattering of fast electrons from a many-body condensed-matter target in a time-periodic light field. At first order in the projectile--target interaction, the general Floquet--Fourier cross section separates into exact laser-dressed projectile kernels and a matrix-valued Floquet density response of the target. For spatially structured or translationally non-invariant systems, the latter is the bi-momentum Floquet structure factor; its momentum diagonal defines the Floquet generalization of the dynamic structure factor, constrained by Hermiticity, positivity, and sum rules. As a controlled realization of the general projectile kernel, an eikonal--Volkov approximation for slowly varying inhomogeneous fields yields a finite-momentum-resolution convolution of the target response. In the homogeneous-field dipole limit, the projectile kernel reduces to Bessel-function sidebands and the cross section takes the familiar Bethe--Floquet form. The Floquet density correlator separates exactly into the outer product of the pump-induced coherent mean density and connected fluctuations. In the straight-trajectory nonrecoil limit, the coherent, target-elastic sector defines the weak-coupling PINEM amplitude; repeated coherent insertions generate the PINEM Bessel ladder, with an explicit no-double-counting prescription for combining this channel with connected losses. As worked examples, we evaluate the connected, target-changing cross section analytically for a metal in the Drude and diffusive limits, recovering Bessel-weighted plasmon-loss and diffusive combs, and for a driven two-level model that exhibits off-diagonal Floquet coherences through Bessel-channel interference.

AI.tldr: The authors generalize the Bethe–Floquet formalism from laser-assisted electron–atom collisions to inelastic scattering of fast electrons from a many-body condensed-matter target in a time-periodic light field, deriving a Floquet–Fourier cross section that factorizes into laser-dressed projectile kernels and a matrix-valued Floquet density response of the target.
AI.motivation: Existing Bethe–Floquet theory was developed for laser-assisted electron–atom collisions, but a corresponding framework for inelastic scattering of fast electrons from many-body condensed-matter targets in a time-periodic light field was lacking, motivating an extension that treats the target's collective and Floquet-coherent response.
AI.method: First-order perturbation theory in the projectile–target interaction combined with Floquet theory; decomposition of the cross section into laser-dressed projectile kernels and a bi-momentum Floquet structure factor; an eikonal–Volkov approximation for slowly varying inhomogeneous fields; homogeneous-field dipole limit; separation of the Floquet density correlator into coherent mean density and connected fluctuations; straight-trajectory nonrecoil limit yielding PINEM amplitudes; analytical evaluation for Drude and diffusive metals and a driven two-level model.
AI.result: The general cross section separates into exact laser-dressed projectile kernels and a matrix-valued Floquet density response; the momentum-diagonal of the bi-momentum Floquet structure factor defines a Floquet dynamic structure factor constrained by Hermiticity, positivity, and sum rules. The eikonal–Volkov kernel gives a finite-momentum-resolution convolution of the target response; the homogeneous-field dipole limit recovers Bessel-function sidebands and the familiar Bethe–Floquet form. The Floquet density correlator splits into an outer product of pump-induced coherent mean density and connected fluctuations. The coherent target-elastic sector defines the weak-coupling PINEM amplitude, with repeated insertions generating the PINEM Bessel ladder and a no-double-counting prescription. Analytic results recover Bessel-weighted plasmon-loss and diffusive combs for Drude/diffusive metals, and off-diagonal Floquet coherences via Bessel-channel interference in a driven two-level model.
AI.conclusion: The extended Bethe–Floquet formalism provides a unified, controlled description of light-driven inelastic electron scattering from condensed-matter targets, connecting laser-dressed projectile kernels, a Floquet density response obeying positivity and sum rules, PINEM ladder physics, and explicit analytic predictions for plasmon-loss and diffusive combs as well as Floquet coherences in a two-level model.

title: Second-order Raman and anharmonic lattice dynamics in lead-halide perovskites
summary: We explore the microscopic origin of THz-driven lattice dynamics in methylammonium lead bromide CH$_3$NH$_3$PbBr$_3$ using two-dimensional THz Kerr-effect spectroscopy. The analysis of the experiment enables discrimination between competing nonlinear excitation mechanisms and reveals that the dominant pathway is phonon-mediated rather than purely photonic. In particular, we argue that the commonly observed 1.15~THz Raman-active $A_g$ mode is not excited directly by the THz electric field. Instead, it emerges through cubic anharmonic coupling to an infrared-active phonon at 0.68~THz. Furthermore, a satellite feature at 1.36~THz is identified as a two-phonon Raman response of the same infrared-active mode. The observation of strong quadratic coupling involving the infrared-active phonon suggests an unconventional form of electron-phonon dressing present in lead-halide perovskites.

AI.tldr: 2D THz Kerr-effect spectroscopy reveals that THz-driven lattice dynamics in CH3NH3PbBr3 are phonon-mediated: the 1.15 THz Ag mode is excited via cubic anharmonic coupling to a 0.68 THz IR-active phonon, and a 1.36 THz satellite is a two-phonon Raman response of the same IR mode, indicating strong quadratic coupling and unconventional electron-phonon dressing.
