title: Orientation refinement for nanobeam precession electron diffraction patterns using spot intensity profiles
summary: We develop a method to measure crystallographic orientations with high angular resolution for nano-beam precession electron diffraction patterns, and applicable to 4D scanning precession electron diffraction. We show that internal variations of intensity in the diffraction spots can be simulated and correlated to experimental variations to measure the crystallographic orientation with a much better angular resolution that with the standard method of automated crystal orientation mapping (ACOM). In a tilt series carried out with long exposure time on a monocrystal of silicon around the main goniometer tilt axis, the imposed tilt angles are retrieved with a 0.044° to 0.054° precision with refinement, against 0.25° to 0.33° with the standard method. Shorter exposure times, introducing Poisson noise, marginally degrade the precision to a 0.054° to 0.066° range. The method also corrects a systematic error of ACOM near zone axis.

AI.tldr: A template-matching method using spot intensity variations in precession electron diffraction patterns achieves ~0.05° orientation precision (vs ~0.3° for ACOM), robust to Poisson noise and correcting a systematic error near zone axis.
AI.motivation: Standard automated crystal orientation mapping (ACOM) offers limited angular resolution for nano-beam precession electron diffraction, which is insufficient for resolving subtle crystallographic orientation variations, particularly in 4D scanning precession electron diffraction datasets.
AI.method: The method simulates internal variations of intensity within diffraction spots and correlates them with experimental patterns to refine crystallographic orientation. It is applicable to 4D scanning precession electron diffraction. Validation used a tilt series on a silicon monocrystal about the main goniometer tilt axis, at long and short exposure times (the latter with Poisson noise).
AI.result: With refinement, imposed tilt angles were retrieved with 0.044°–0.054° precision (long exposure) versus 0.25°–0.33° for the standard ACOM method. Shorter exposures degraded precision only marginally, to 0.054°–0.066°. The method also corrects a systematic ACOM error near the zone axis.
AI.conclusion: Correlating simulated and experimental intra-spot intensity variations provides a substantially higher angular resolution than standard ACOM for nano-beam precession electron diffraction, is applicable to 4D scanning datasets, is robust to Poisson noise, and removes a systematic near-zone-axis bias.

title: Extracting the anyon charge from shot noise in complex fractional quantum Hall edges
summary: Shot-noise measurements with a quantum point contact provide a direct probe of the quasiparticle charge in Laughlin fractional quantum Hall (FQH) states. However, the interpretation of such measurements becomes more subtle for multichannel edges, where the point-contact tunneling noise coexists with noise generated by intermode equilibration and heating. We develop a general framework that incorporates both these contributions and apply it to the paradigmatic $ν=2/3$ FQH edge. We derive expressions for the drain auto- and cross-correlations in a four-terminal QPC geometry and show that equilibration-induced heating affects the auto- and cross-correlations in parametrically different way than the intrinsic partition noise. This distinction permits us to propose a specific combination of the two correlations which strongly suppresses the heating contribution and fully recovers the tunneling quasiparticle charge. Our results thereby provide a systematic framework for interpreting shot-noise measurements in complex FQH edges and can be further extended to more general counterpropagating edge structures.

AI.tldr: The paper develops a general theoretical framework for shot-noise measurements in multichannel fractional quantum Hall edges, incorporating both point-contact partition noise and intermode equilibration/heating noise, and applies it to the ν=2/3 edge to extract the quasiparticle charge.
AI.motivation: Shot-noise measurements via a quantum point contact directly probe quasiparticle charge in Laughlin FQH states, but for multichannel edges the tunneling noise coexists with noise from intermode equilibration and heating, making interpretation subtle.
AI.method: The authors develop a general framework incorporating both partition noise and equilibration/heating contributions, derive expressions for drain auto- and cross-correlations in a four-terminal QPC geometry, and apply it to the paradigmatic ν=2/3 FQH edge.
AI.result: Equilibration-induced heating affects the auto- and cross-correlations in a parametrically different way than the intrinsic partition noise, which allows the authors to propose a specific combination of the two correlations that strongly suppresses the heating contribution and fully recovers the tunneling quasiparticle charge.
AI.conclusion: The work provides a systematic framework for interpreting shot-noise measurements in complex FQH edges and can be extended to more general counterpropagating edge structures.

title: Bogoliubov self-consistent $GW$ and second-order Green's function methods for attractive fermionic interactions
summary: Describing fermionic systems with attractive interactions, such as superconductors and atomic nuclei, beyond the mean-field level remains a central challenge. In this work, we investigate the performance of Bogoliubov fully self-consistent $GW$ (Bog.~sc$GW$) and second-order Green's function (Bog.~scGF2) methods, implemented within a unified imaginary-time and imaginary-frequency framework. Using the attractive Hubbard model as a benchmark against full configuration interaction (FCI), we find that Bog. scGF2 provides a more accurate description than Bog.~sc$GW$. In particular, Bog.~sc$GW$ systematically overestimates the correlation energy, with errors increasing rapidly as the attractive interaction strength grows. These results highlight the importance of exchange contributions in strongly correlated fermionic systems, even when exchange effects are included only at low order in perturbation theory.

AI.tldr: This work benchmarks Bogoliubov self-consistent GW (Bog. scGW) and second-order Green's function (Bog. scGF2) methods for attractive fermionic systems using the Hubbard model against FCI, finding Bog. scGF2 more accurate while Bog. scGW systematically overestimates correlation energy.
AI.motivation: Describing fermionic systems with attractive interactions (superconductors, atomic nuclei) beyond the mean-field level is a central challenge, motivating the need to assess the accuracy of self-consistent many-body methods in this regime.
AI.method: Bogoliubov fully self-consistent GW (Bog. scGW) and second-order Green's function (Bog. scGF2) methods, implemented within a unified imaginary-time and imaginary-frequency framework, were applied to the attractive Hubbard model and benchmarked against full configuration interaction (FCI).
AI.result: Bog. scGF2 provides a more accurate description than Bog. scGW. Bog. scGW systematically overestimates the correlation energy, with errors increasing rapidly as the attractive interaction strength grows.
AI.conclusion: Exchange contributions are important in strongly correlated fermionic systems, even when included only at low order in perturbation theory.

title: Optimizing the magnetic hyperthermia efficiency from the structural dependence of dipolar interactions in magnetic nanoparticles assemblies
summary: Magnetic hyperthermia, based on the conversion of the magnetic energy of magnetic nanoparticles (MNP) under an alternating external field into heat, presents a great interest, especially because of important applications such as promising advances in cancer treatment. The underlying frequency-dependent response of the MNP assembly under the excitation field depends on the first hand on the individual properties of the MNP such as their size, shape and magnetocrystalline anisotropy and on the other hand on collective properties generated by interactions between MNP. Due to the long-range dipolar component of the latter, the first consequence is the so-called demagnetizing effects, making the response dependent on the external sample shape. This is the reason for studying the properties of MNP in assemblies of anisotropic external shapes such as films, chains, or elongated aggregates. In the present work, using a recently developed Time Quantified Monte Carlo (TQMC) framework for dynamic simulations, we focus more precisely on the importance of the local structure in such anisotropic aggregates to the dipolar interactions contribution of the response to the external field. Here the local structure is understood as both the location of the nanoparticles and the distribution of their easy axes. We show that the latter must be determined in a self-consistent way starting with the equilibrium structure of a ferrofluid modeled as the dipolar hard sphere fluid.

AI.tldr: This work uses a Time Quantified Monte Carlo framework to show that the dipolar-interaction contribution to the magnetic hyperthermia response of anisotropic MNP aggregates depends critically on local structure—both particle positions and easy-axis distribution.
AI.motivation: Magnetic hyperthermia, converting magnetic energy of nanoparticles into heat under an alternating field, is promising for cancer treatment. The frequency-dependent response of an MNP assembly depends on individual particle properties (size, shape, magnetocrystalline anisotropy) and on collective inter-particle interactions. Long-range dipolar interactions cause demagnetizing effects that make the response depend on the external sample shape, motivating the study of assemblies with anisotropic external shapes (films, chains, elongated aggregates).
AI.method: Dynamic simulations are performed using a recently developed Time Quantified Monte Carlo (TQMC) framework, applied to anisotropic aggregates of magnetic nanoparticles, focusing on the role of local structure in the dipolar-interaction contribution to the response. Local structure is defined as both nanoparticle locations and the distribution of their easy axes; the easy-axis distribution is determined self-consistently starting from the equilibrium structure of a ferrofluid modeled as a dipolar hard sphere fluid.
AI.result: The dipolar-interaction contribution to the response to the external field is strongly governed by the local structure of the anisotropic aggregates, encompassing both particle positions and easy-axis distribution. The easy-axis distribution must be determined self-consistently, beginning from the equilibrium structure of the dipolar hard sphere fluid.
AI.conclusion: Local structure—particle arrangement and easy-axis distribution—is essential for accurately describing dipolar interactions in anisotropic MNP aggregates relevant to magnetic hyperthermia. A self-consistent determination of the easy-axis distribution, rooted in the equilibrium ferrofluid structure, is required for reliable modeling.

title: Electronic Density versus Geometry for Machine-Learned Molecular Absorption Spectra
summary: Molecular optical absorption spectroscopy provides a direct probe of electronic structure and is widely used for molecular identification, interpretation of photophysical behaviour, and planning of spectroscopy experiments. Calculating the absorption spectra using first-principle excited-state methods, however, is computationally demanding, at least compared to ground-state calculations, which limits their routine application across large molecular sets. Machine-learning (ML) surrogates can reduce this cost and allow rapid spectral prediction. However, their performance depends strongly on how molecular information is represented. Here, we compare using the ground-state electron density versus the molecular geometry as inputs to a ML model for predicting absorption spectra, for a training set of 6874 molecules selected from the QM7 dataset. For each of these molecules, the density was calculated using density functional theory (DFT) and the absorption spectrum was calculated using linear-response (LR) time-dependent DFT (TDDFT). Utilizing the ground-state density as the input to the ML model is motivated by the Hohenberg-Kohn and Runge-Gross theorems, and the fact that the ground-state density encodes information about bonding, charge localisation, and electronic delocalisation. Hence, it may be a more judicious starting point for the ML model compared to the geometry, as it effectively decouples the chemistry of the ground-state. The question we test is whether the benefits of using the density outweigh the (notprohibitive) penalty of requiring an additional single-point DFT calculation for the density. We find that the density-based convolutional neural network achieves a validation correlation of 0.9926, compared with 0.9795 for the best geometry-based graph model, reducing the residual decorrelation, by approximately 64%.

AI.tldr: Comparing ground-state electron density vs. molecular geometry as ML inputs for predicting absorption spectra of 6874 QM7 molecules, a density-based CNN outperforms the best geometry-based graph model.
AI.motivation: First-principle excited-state methods for calculating absorption spectra are computationally demanding, limiting routine application across large molecular sets. ML surrogates can reduce cost, but their performance depends strongly on molecular representation. The authors test whether the ground-state electron density, motivated by the Hohenberg-Kohn and Runge-Gross theorems and its encoding of bonding, charge localisation, and delocalisation, is a more judicious input than molecular geometry, and whether its benefits outweigh the cost of an extra single-point DFT calculation.
AI.method: For a training set of 6874 molecules from the QM7 dataset, ground-state densities were computed with DFT and absorption spectra with linear-response TDDFT. Two ML input representations were compared: the ground-state electron density fed to a convolutional neural network, versus the molecular geometry fed to a graph-based model.
AI.result: The density-based CNN achieved a validation correlation of 0.9926, compared with 0.9795 for the best geometry-based graph model, reducing the residual decorrelation by approximately 64%.
AI.conclusion: Using the ground-state electron density as the ML input yields more accurate absorption-spectrum predictions than molecular geometry, and the accuracy gain outweighs the (non-prohibitive) penalty of requiring an additional single-point DFT calculation for the density.

title: Ab initio design of enhanced and sign-reversible spin Hall and spin Nernst conductivity in skutterudite materials
summary: The search for novel materials capable of robust spin-current generation remains an active area of research. Here, we investigate the intrinsic spin Hall and spin Nernst effects in Co- and Rh-based skutterudites and explore their enhancement through heavy-metal substitution and site-selective doping. Using first-principles calculations and Wannier-based tight-binding models, we analyze the spin Berry curvature and spin-transport responses of pristine MX$_3$, where M = Co, Rh and X = As, Sb, as well as chemically modified systems. Despite sizable momentum-resolved spin Berry curvature, the pristine compounds exhibit relatively small net spin Hall responses due to substantial cancellation across the Brillouin zone. Isoelectronic Ir and Bi substitution at 8$c$ Wycoff M site produces little enhancement near the E$_F$, whereas non-isoelectronic Pt substitution yields a relatively better response. Most interestingly, the incorporation of Pt at the interstitial $2a$ Wycoff site of RhAs$_3$ nearly doubles the spin Hall conductivity to $\sim400~(\hbar/e)(Ω,\mathrm{cm})^{-1}$ near the E$_F$ when compared to Pt substitution at 8$c$ position. At 300 K, the same interstitially filled system exhibits a spin Nernst conductivity of $\sim1.46~(\hbar/e),\mathrm{A,m^{-1}K^{-1}}$ at the E$_F$, nearly an order of magnitude larger than that of $M$-site Pt substitution. The enhanced responses arise from Pt $5d$ states, strong spin-orbit coupling, and avoided crossings that generate pronounced spin-Berry-curvature hot spots. These results demonstrate that site-selective chemical engineering can effectively overcome momentum-space cancellation resulting in enhanced spin Hall and spin Nernst responses in skutterudites. Our results provide a possible route towards robust spin-current generation in this class of materials.

AI.tldr: Co- and Rh-based skutterudites show momentum-space cancellation of spin Berry curvature that limits pristine spin Hall responses; site-selective interstitial Pt doping at the 2a site of RhAs3 nearly doubles spin Hall conductivity (~400 (ℏ/e)(Ω·cm)⁻¹) and yields spin Nernst conductivity ~1.46 (ℏ/e) A m⁻¹ K⁻¹, overcoming cancellation via Pt 5d states, strong SOC, and avoided crossings.
AI.motivation: Robust spin-current generation requires novel materials, and skutterudites are promising candidates for intrinsic spin Hall and spin Nernst effects; the authors aim to understand and overcome the cancellation of spin Berry curvature that suppresses net responses, and to test whether heavy-metal substitution and site-selective doping can enhance spin-transport.
AI.method: First-principles calculations combined with Wannier-based tight-binding models were used to compute the spin Berry curvature and spin-transport responses of pristine MX3 (M = Co, Rh; X = As, Sb) and chemically modified systems, comparing isoelectronic Ir and Bi substitution at the 8c M site, non-isoelectronic Pt substitution, and interstitial Pt incorporation at the 2a Wyckoff site of RhAs3.
AI.result: Pristine compounds have sizable momentum-resolved spin Berry curvature but small net spin Hall responses due to substantial Brillouin-zone cancellation. Isoelectronic Ir and Bi substitution at 8c gives little enhancement near EF, while non-isoelectronic Pt substitution performs better. Interstitial Pt at 2a in RhAs3 nearly doubles spin Hall conductivity to ~400 (ℏ/e)(Ω·cm)⁻¹ near EF relative to 8c Pt substitution, and at 300 K shows spin Nernst conductivity ~1.46 (ℏ/e) A m⁻¹ K⁻¹, nearly an order of magnitude larger than M-site Pt substitution. The enhancement stems from Pt 5d states, strong spin-orbit coupling, and avoided crossings producing pronounced spin-Berry-curvature hot spots.
AI.conclusion: Site-selective chemical engineering can effectively overcome momentum-space cancellation of spin Berry curvature, enabling enhanced spin Hall and spin Nernst responses in skutterudites and offering a route toward robust spin-current generation in this material class.

title: Evaluating Chern Topology in Discretized Brillouin Zones Using Bargmann Invariants
summary: We develop a finite-state geometric framework based on third-order Bargmann invariants for evaluating Chern numbers and characterizing local quantum-state geometry. Using gauge-invariant state overlaps, the framework evaluates the Chern number directly on discretized parameter spaces while retaining local geometric information through the phase-derived density and the complementary amplitude density, as well as signatures associated with changes in topological character. We apply the construction to the Qi--Wu--Zhang, $1/3$- and $1/4$-flux Hofstadter, SSH, and Rice--Mele models, including a rank-$2$ extension for isolated composite subspaces and applications to closed-loop and parameter-space topology. The resulting framework organizes Chern topology and local geometric information directly from finite-state data, providing a compact state-based description without relying on dynamical evolution.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a finite-state geometric framework using third-order Bargmann invariants and gauge-invariant state overlaps to evaluate Chern numbers and characterize local quantum-state geometry on discretized parameter spaces.
AI.motivation: Conventional Chern number evaluation often relies on dynamical evolution or Berry-curvature integration, which complicates direct extraction from finite-state data. A state-based, gauge-invariant description is desirable for compactly organizing topological and local geometric information.
AI.method: The authors construct a finite-state geometric framework based on third-order Bargmann invariants. Using gauge-invariant state overlaps, they compute the Chern number directly on discretized parameter spaces while retaining local geometric information via a phase-derived density and a complementary amplitude density, along with signatures of topological-character changes. They also develop a rank-2 extension for isolated composite subspaces.
AI.result: The framework is applied to the Qi-Wu-Zhang model, 1/3- and 1/4-flux Hofstadter models, SSH, and Rice-Mele models, including closed-loop and parameter-space topology, successfully yielding Chern numbers and local geometric diagnostics from finite-state data.
AI.conclusion: Chern topology and local geometric information can be organized directly from finite-state data, providing a compact state-based description that avoids reliance on dynamical evolution.

title: Uniform instanton theory for bridge-mediated nonadiabatic tunneling
summary: Instanton theory provides a semiclassical approximation to nonadiabatic rate constants within a path-integral framework and captures nuclear quantum effects such as tunneling and zero-point energy. Although the simplest reactions proceed directly from reactants to products, a number of important nonadiabatic processes involve three electronic states and react via a concerted mechanism through a virtual bridge state, also referred to as bridge-mediated tunneling or superexchange. In previous work, we have derived an instanton theory to describe such reactions using a dominant tunneling trajectory that propagates on each of the three potential energy surfaces. However, this approach is only valid when the bridge state is sufficiently low in energy. In contrast, in the high-bridge regime, the trajectories on the bridge surface become infinitesimally short, which causes the previous theory to break down. In this work, we derive the appropriate asymptotic approximation for the high-bridge regime and find that the resulting theory reduces to a two-state golden-rule instanton with an effective coupling that describes a nonresonant hop to the virtual bridge state. We further develop a uniform asymptotic instanton theory that eliminates divergences and smoothly connects the high- and low-bridge regimes. In a companion paper, we apply the method to study the quintet-to-singlet transition (via a triplet bridge) of an iron(II) complex.

AI.tldr: This work derives a uniform asymptotic instanton theory for three-state nonadiabatic reactions that smoothly connects the low- and high-bridge regimes, showing the high-bridge limit reduces to an effective two-state golden-rule instanton.
AI.motivation: Prior instanton theory for bridge-mediated (superexchange) three-state nonadiabatic reactions relied on a dominant tunneling trajectory on each of the three potential energy surfaces, but it is valid only when the bridge state is sufficiently low in energy. In the high-bridge regime the bridge-surface trajectories become infinitesimally short, causing the previous theory to break down. A correct asymptotic description for this regime was needed.
AI.method: The authors derive the appropriate asymptotic approximation for the high-bridge regime within a path-integral instanton framework, then construct a uniform asymptotic instanton theory that removes the divergences and interpolates continuously between the high- and low-bridge limits.
AI.result: The high-bridge asymptotic theory reduces to a two-state golden-rule instanton with an effective coupling describing a nonresonant hop to the virtual bridge state. The uniform asymptotic instanton theory eliminates divergences and smoothly connects the high- and low-bridge regimes.
AI.conclusion: The uniform asymptotic instanton theory provides a consistent semiclassical treatment of concerted three-state nonadiabatic reactions across both bridge-energy regimes, and is applied in a companion paper to the quintet-to-singlet transition (via a triplet bridge) of an iron(II) complex.

title: Coercivity-Aware Machine Learning Discovery of Rare-Earth-Free Soft Magnetic Alloys with First-Principles Magnetic Benchmarks
summary: Coercivity-aware machine learning is developed to screen rare-earth-free soft magnetic alloys using Curie temperature and coercivity as coupled design targets. A compiled experimental magnetic-material dataset is evaluated using composition-grouped partitioning to avoid overlap of identical compositions between training and testing, and elemental fractions and composition-weighted elemental descriptors are examined for prediction of the two magnetic properties. Residual-based prediction intervals and distance-to-training filters are then incorporated to screen Fe-Co-Ni-Mn-Al-Si compositions. Composition-grouped evaluation shows lower predictive accuracy than conventional random partitioning, demonstrating the importance of evaluating transfer to previously unseen compositions. Combining weighted elemental descriptors with elemental fractions improves Curie-temperature prediction, whereas the additional descriptors do not improve coercivity prediction, consistent with the strong dependence of coercivity on processing and microstructure. Uncertainty-aware screening substantially narrows the candidate space and identifies Fe-Co-rich compositions for further evaluation. First-principles calculations independently show strong magnetic polarization and magnetovolume effects in representative Fe-Co structures, while finite-temperature atomistic spin simulations place the Fe-Co benchmark systems on high magnetic-ordering-temperature scales. The combined approach provides a computational framework for prioritizing rare-earth-free soft-magnetic chemistries while distinguishing composition-level screening from candidate-specific physical validation.

AI.tldr: This work builds a coercivity-aware, uncertainty-quantified machine-learning screening framework for rare-earth-free soft magnetic alloys, jointly targeting Curie temperature and coercivity. Composition-grouped validation reveals reduced accuracy versus random splits, and uncertainty filters narrow candidates to Fe-Co-rich compositions validated via first-principles and atomistic spin simulations.
AI.motivation: Rare-earth-free soft magnetic alloys are attractive alternatives to rare-earth-containing magnets, but designing them requires balancing two coupled magnetic properties: high Curie temperature and low coercivity. Conventional random data partitioning overestimates model transferability to unseen chemistries, so a more realistic, composition-grouped evaluation and an uncertainty-aware screening strategy are needed to prioritize candidate chemistries reliably.
AI.method: A compiled experimental magnetic-material dataset is used. Composition-grouped partitioning prevents identical compositions from appearing in both training and testing. Inputs combine elemental fractions with composition-weighted elemental descriptors. Models predict Curie temperature and coercivity; residual-based prediction intervals and distance-to-training filters are applied to screen Fe-Co-Ni-Mn-Al-Si compositions. Representative Fe-Co structures are then examined with first-principles calculations and finite-temperature atomistic spin simulations.
AI.result: Composition-grouped evaluation yields lower predictive accuracy than conventional random partitioning. Weighted elemental descriptors plus elemental fractions improve Curie-temperature prediction, but the extra descriptors do not improve coercivity prediction. Uncertainty-aware screening substantially narrows the candidate space and highlights Fe-Co-rich compositions. First-principles calculations show strong magnetic polarization and magnetovolume effects in representative Fe-Co structures, and atomistic spin simulations place Fe-Co benchmarks at high magnetic-ordering-temperature scales.
AI.conclusion: Coercivity-aware machine learning with composition-grouped validation and uncertainty quantification offers a practical computational framework for prioritizing rare-earth-free soft-magnetic chemistries, while clearly separating composition-level screening from candidate-specific physical validation.

title: Plasmon modes in tilted three-dimensional nodal-ring semimetals. II. Vortex nodal ring
summary: We investigate collective charge excitations in three-dimensional vortex nodal-ring semimetals (VNRs), whose pseudospin texture winds around the nodal ring and differs qualitatively from that of the conventional $\mathcal{PT}$-symmetric nodal-ring semimetal (PTNR). While plasmon modes in PTNRs have been studied in a companion work, arXiv:2609.35373. Here, we focus on how a VNR's pseudospin texture changes the response compared with the former. Within a low-energy two-band description and the random-phase approximation, we analyse the density response, density-of-states, Drude weights, dielectric function, and plasmon modes at low doping. We consider the untilted system together with in-plane and axial band-tilts. Although the VNR and PTNR have distinct Hamiltonians, pseudospin textures, and Berry-curvature distributions, their linearised energy dispersions coincide. The vortex texture, however, introduces a toroidal-angle dependence in the band-overlap factor and quantum metric, thereby modifying the charge response. We examine how these effects enter the dielectric screening and collective modes for different wavevector orientations. Our results clarify how pseudospin texture, beyond the band dispersion alone, influences collective charge dynamics in three-dimensional nodal-ring semimetals.

AI.tldr: This work analyzes collective charge excitations (plasmons) in three-dimensional vortex nodal-ring semimetals (VNRs), showing how the vortex pseudospin texture alters the charge response relative to conventional PT-symmetric nodal-ring semimetals (PTNRs) despite identical linearized band dispersions.
AI.motivation: VNRs possess a pseudospin texture winding around the nodal ring that differs qualitatively from PTNRs. Although plasmons in PTNRs were treated in a companion work (arXiv:2609.35373), it is unclear how the distinct vortex pseudospin texture modifies the dielectric and collective charge response, since the two systems share the same linearized energy dispersions. This motivates isolating the role of pseudospin texture and quantum geometry beyond band dispersion.
AI.method: A low-energy two-band model combined with the random-phase approximation (RPA) is used. The authors compute the density response, density of states, Drude weights, dielectric function, and plasmon modes at low doping, considering the untilted case as well as in-plane and axial band tilts, and examining different wavevector orientations.
AI.result: Although VNR and PTNR have distinct Hamiltonians, pseudospin textures, and Berry-curvature distributions, their linearized energy dispersions coincide. The vortex texture induces a toroidal-angle dependence in the band-overlap factor and quantum metric, which modifies the charge response. These effects enter the dielectric screening and collective modes in a wavevector-orientation-dependent manner.
AI.conclusion: Pseudospin texture, beyond band dispersion alone, governs collective charge dynamics in three-dimensional nodal-ring semimetals, clarifying how vortex versus PT-symmetric textures produce distinguishable plasmon behavior.

title: CIS(2): a state-specific, size-intensive perturbative correction to configuration interaction singles
summary: We present a state-specific second-order perturbation theory based on a configuration interaction singles (CIS) reference and its generalized Fock operator. Starting from a fully internally contracted construction, we retain the complete doubles space and internally contracted triples in the first-order wave function. We consider two partitions, Canonical and Block-diagonal, with reference excitation energies given by the Fock excitation gap $ω^{(0)}$ and the CIS excitation energy $ω_{\rm CIS}$, respectively. Our analysis establishes that strict size-intensivity is preserved when the contracted-triples denominators use bare Fock gaps and the occupied--virtual Fock block is projected to remove residual spectator coupling. Based on this observation, combining Canonical triples with Block-diagonal doubles yields a size-intensive Hybrid partition. These properties are verified for water with non-interacting helium atoms. Our formulation enables $O(o^3v^2)$ cost per matrix--vector product in a semicanonical basis. On the QUEST\#1 benchmark, Canonical and Block-diagonal show opposite systematic biases, whereas Hybrid gives the best overall accuracy among the three partitions. Its mean absolute errors for singlets and triplets are 0.24 and 0.15~eV, compared with 0.28 and 0.22~eV for CIS(D). The improvement is largest for Rydberg excitations, although CIS(D) remains more accurate for valence singlets.

AI.tldr: A state-specific second-order perturbation theory on a CIS reference, with two partition schemes and a size-intensive Hybrid partition, gives O(o^3v^2) matrix–vector cost and best overall accuracy on QUEST#1.
AI.motivation: Second-order perturbation corrections to a CIS reference are attractive for excited states, but their formal properties (especially size-intensivity) and accuracy depend heavily on how the zeroth-order Hamiltonian is partitioned. The paper aims to define size-intensive partitions and assess their accuracy.
AI.method: Fully internally contracted CIS-based second-order perturbation theory retaining the complete doubles space and internally contracted triples in the first-order wave function. Two partitions are considered: Canonical (Fock excitation gap omega^(0)) and Block-diagonal (CIS excitation energy omega_CIS). Size-intensivity is enforced by using bare Fock gaps in the contracted-triples denominators and projecting the occupied-virtual Fock block to remove spectator coupling; combining Canonical triples with Block-diagonal doubles yields a Hybrid partition.
AI.result: Size-intensivity is verified for water with non-interacting helium atoms. The formulation is O(o^3v^2) per matrix-vector product in a semicanonical basis. On QUEST#1, Canonical and Block-diagonal show opposite systematic biases; Hybrid is most accurate overall, with mean absolute errors of 0.24 eV (singlets) and 0.15 eV (triplets) versus 0.28 and 0.22 eV for CIS(D). Gains are largest for Rydberg excitations, while CIS(D) remains better for valence singlets.
AI.conclusion: Partition choice governs both formal size-intensivity and accuracy. A Hybrid partition (Canonical triples + Block-diagonal doubles) preserves strict size-intensivity and outperforms CIS(D) overall for excitation energies in benchmark tests.

title: Algebra of symmetry allowed physical properties of crystals
summary: The symmetry of a physical system given by the 122 magnetic point groups (MPGs) leads to only 21 sets of restrictions on any physical tensors. Those, so called, tenor forms were labeled by letters from A to U by R. R. Birss (Symmetry and Magnetism, North Holland, Amsterdam, 1964). A new concept of property-related point groups (PRPGs) is proposed. It is shown that the 21 PRPGs isomorphic to the 21 non-centrosymmetric crystallographic point groups (CPGs) corresponds to the 21 tensor forms. Therefore instead of a symbols from A to U one can use PRPGs as mathematical objects corresponding to the tenor forms. From the Neumann's principle given multipole component is only allowed in a system when a group describing symmetry of the system is a subgroup of the multipole component symmetry. Each tensor can be expressed in the terms of the multipole degrees of freedom, i.e. it corresponds to a subset of all multipole components allowed by given PRPG. Those relations leads to the algebra of tensor forms, where space of allowed tensor components and space of PRPG operators are somehow dual to each other.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces property-related point groups (PRPGs) as a new framework for classifying the 21 tensor forms (Birss's A–U labels) in magnetically ordered crystals, showing that each tensor form corresponds to one of 21 PRPGs isomorphic to the 21 non-centrosymmetric crystallographic point groups.
AI.motivation: The 122 magnetic point groups impose only 21 distinct sets of restrictions on physical tensors, traditionally labeled A–U by Birss. These abstract letter labels lack a clear mathematical-object interpretation. The paper seeks a more meaningful, symmetry-based representation of tensor forms that connects directly to group-theoretical structures and multipole degrees of freedom.
AI.method: The author proposes the concept of property-related point groups (PRPGs). It is demonstrated that the 21 PRPGs, which are isomorphic to the 21 non-centrosymmetric crystallographic point groups (CPGs), map one-to-one onto the 21 tensor forms. Multipole degrees of freedom are used to express each tensor as a subset of allowed multipole components, and Neumann's principle is applied to link the symmetry group of a system to the symmetry of the multipole components.
AI.result: The 21 tensor forms are shown to correspond exactly to the 21 PRPGs, allowing replacement of Birss's A–U symbols with PRPGs as mathematical objects. Each tensor corresponds to a subset of multipole components allowed by its PRPG. An algebra of tensor forms emerges in which the space of allowed tensor components and the space of PRPG operators are dual to each other.
AI.conclusion: The PRPG framework provides a group-theoretical and multipole-based reformulation of tensor forms in magnetic crystals, offering a mathematically grounded alternative to the conventional A–U notation and establishing a duality between tensor-component spaces and PRPG operator spaces.

title: Beyond Pure Dephasing: Quantum Error Correction in Single Molecules Requires Multiple Spins
summary: We propose multi-spin molecules as a viable architecture for fault-tolerant quantum computing. To this aim, we introduce a correction protocol handling both diagonal and off-diagonal errors, typically associated with dephasing and relaxation. The scheme is based on a hybrid encoding which combines dephasing-tolerant units suppressing the leading pure dephasing error into a multi-spin molecule implementing a multi-qubit code for residual off-diagonal errors. Our proposal leverages peculiar properties of molecular spins, i.e. the strong hierarchy between different errors and the possibility to engineer multi-spin molecules at the synthetic level. Moreover, it addresses the important issue of the loss of coherences in anharmonic systems subject to off-diagonal errors, which hampers their correction at the single spin level. Thanks to the huge suppression of dephasing by the first-level code, we numerically demonstrate the potential performance of this strategy even with a limited number of spins per logical unit.

AI.tldr: The abstract proposes multi-spin molecules as a fault-tolerant quantum computing architecture, using a hybrid encoding with dephasing-tolerant units within a multi-spin molecular multi-qubit code to correct both diagonal and off-diagonal errors.
AI.motivation: Fault-tolerant quantum computing requires handling both dephasing (diagonal) and relaxation (off-diagonal) errors. A key obstacle is the loss of coherences in anharmonic systems subject to off-diagonal errors, which prevents their correction at the single-spin level. Molecular spins offer exploitable properties, such as a strong hierarchy between different errors and synthetic engineerability, motivating a tailored architecture.
AI.method: The authors introduce a correction protocol addressing diagonal and off-diagonal errors simultaneously, based on a hybrid encoding. Dephasing-tolerant units suppress the leading pure dephasing error, and these units are combined into a multi-spin molecule implementing a multi-qubit code for residual off-diagonal errors. The design exploits the strong hierarchy between errors and the ability to engineer multi-spin molecules at the synthetic level. Numerical simulations assess performance.
AI.result: Thanks to the large suppression of dephasing achieved by the first-level code, numerical results demonstrate the potential performance of the strategy even with a limited number of spins per logical unit.
AI.conclusion: Multi-spin molecules combined with a hybrid encoding scheme constitute a viable route toward fault-tolerant quantum computing, correcting both dephasing and relaxation errors and enabling effective error correction despite a small number of spins per logical unit.

title: Complete Magnetic Hierarchy in Bichromatically Driven Unconventional Magnets
summary: We establish a general framework for engineering unconventional magnetism using bichromatic driving. We identify a sharp hierarchy: for a bichromatic drive with a generic even commensurate frequency ratio, the leading continuum $q$-wave magnet generates components only up to order $q-2$, whereas lattice higher-gradient terms supply the missing $q-1$ and $q$ parities and complete the hierarchy through order $q$. We explicitly illustrate this new revised hierarchy on a $d$-wave altermagnet irradiated by a circularly-linearly polarized light, and show that the asymmetry of the driving field is transferred to the light-dressed electronic structure, producing momentum-asymmetric dispersions beyond the static and single-frequency limits. We further show that this band asymmetry is absent in the leading continuum expansion and originates from higher-gradient lattice terms that are converted by the bichromatic drive into odd-in-momentum contributions. Extending the analysis to higher-order unconventional magnets, we further obtain complete magnetic hierarchies for all $q$-parity unconventional magnets. Our results establish bichromatic Floquet driving as a general route for generating mixed-parity magnetic hierarchies and dynamically engineering unconventional magnetism.

AI.tldr: The paper develops a general Floquet framework showing that bichromatic driving engineers unconventional magnetism with a sharp parity hierarchy: a generic even commensurate frequency ratio yields a leading q-wave magnet whose components extend only to order q-2, while higher-gradient lattice terms supply the missing q-1 and q parities, completing the hierarchy up to order q. Illustrated on a d-wave altermagnet under circularly-linearly polarized light, the drive transfers its asymmetry to the light-dressed band structure, producing momentum-asymmetric dispersions that originate from lattice higher-gradient terms converted into odd-in-momentum contributions.
AI.motivation: Conventional routes to unconventional magnetism are largely limited to static or single-frequency drives, which restrict the achievable magnetic symmetries and parities. The authors aim to establish a general, systematic route for dynamically generating mixed-parity magnetic hierarchies and controlling band asymmetry beyond the static and single-frequency limits.
AI.method: The authors construct a general framework for bichromatic Floquet driving with a generic even commensurate frequency ratio. They analyze the parity structure of the leading continuum q-wave magnet versus lattice higher-gradient terms, deriving a revised hierarchy that extends the accessible components up to order q. The framework is explicitly applied to a d-wave altermagnet irradiated by circularly-linearly polarized light, and generalized to higher-order unconventional magnets to obtain complete magnetic hierarchies for all q-parity magnets.
AI.result: For an even commensurate frequency ratio, the leading continuum q-wave magnet generates components only up to order q-2, while lattice higher-gradient terms supply the missing q-1 and q parities, completing the hierarchy through order q. In the d-wave altermagnet case, the driving-field asymmetry is transferred to the light-dressed electronic structure, yielding momentum-asymmetric dispersions absent in the static and single-frequency limits. This band asymmetry is absent in the leading continuum expansion and arises from higher-gradient lattice terms converted by the bichromatic drive into odd-in-momentum contributions. Complete magnetic hierarchies are obtained for all q-parity unconventional magnets.
AI.conclusion: Bichromatic Floquet driving provides a general route for generating mixed-parity magnetic hierarchies and dynamically engineering unconventional magnetism, extending achievable magnetic symmetries beyond static and single-frequency driving schemes.

title: Illuminating early ZrC oxidation using ensemble small-cell DFT with dynamic gas management
summary: During zirconium carbide oxidation, liberated carbon can remain beneath the oxide or escape as gas, complicating the interpretation of mass measurements. We adapt the small-cell ensemble method using sixteen 140 ps ab initio molecular dynamics trajectories at 873-1273 K under a sustained high oxygen flux with gas removal. The average rates of net mass gain and total carbon transfer into gas or retained chains follow Arrhenius trends. Above 973 K, gas evolution levels off while total carbon transfer increases. The fraction of transferred carbon retained in chains rises from 40 % at 973 K to 66 % at 1273 K. Fits after 40 ps suggest declining carbon transfer rates over time, although not in every trajectory. These results show that carbon partitioning during early oxidation depends on temperature, with increasing temperature above 973 K favouring chain formation over gasification.

AI.tldr: Small-cell AIMD simulations (16 × 140 ps, 873–1273 K) under sustained high O flux reveal temperature-dependent carbon partitioning during early ZrC oxidation: above 973 K gas evolution plateaus while chain retention rises from 40% to 66%.
AI.motivation: Mass measurements during zirconium carbide (ZrC) oxidation are hard to interpret because liberated carbon either stays beneath the oxide or escapes as gas, making net mass change an ambiguous signal. A mechanistic, atomic-scale understanding of how this carbon partitions is needed.
AI.method: Adapted small-cell ensemble approach with sixteen 140 ps ab initio molecular dynamics (AIMD) trajectories at 873–1273 K, using a sustained high oxygen flux with gas removal to mimic oxidation conditions. Net mass gain and total carbon transfer (to gas or retained chains) were tracked and fitted to Arrhenius trends; time-dependent fits were performed after 40 ps.
AI.result: Average rates of net mass gain and total carbon transfer (gas plus retained chains) follow Arrhenius behavior. Above 973 K, gas evolution levels off while total carbon transfer keeps increasing. The fraction of transferred carbon retained in chains grows from 40% at 973 K to 66% at 1273 K. Fits after 40 ps indicate declining carbon transfer rates over time, though not in every trajectory.
AI.conclusion: Carbon partitioning during early ZrC oxidation is temperature-dependent: increasing temperature above 973 K favors chain formation over gasification, which helps explain the complexity of interpreting mass-change measurements.

title: Electrostatic Doping of Moiré Superlattices Controls the Optical Fingerprint of a WSe_2 /Twisted Bilayer Graphene heterostructure
summary: We theoretically investigate the optical response of the WSe2 monolayer vertically stacked on twisted bilayer graphene (tBG) under electrostatic doping. In this heterostructure, the doped moiré superlattice of tBG generates a spatially modulated electrostatic potential that couples to the electron and hole constituents of the WSe2 exciton through the screened Coulomb interaction, thereby providing a microscopic mechanism for exciton coupling to the charge-density landscape of the moiré Fermi sea. Focusing on twist angles below the magic angle (1.1°), where electronic correlations are strongly enhanced, we demonstrate that electrostatic doping induces pronounced modifications of the excitonic absorption spectrum, including the emergence of multiple satellite resonances. We show that these spectral features originate from the interplay between the exciton center-of-mass and internal degrees of freedom, together with doping-induced hybridization between Rydberg exciton states of different orbital symmetry. The calculated spectra are in good agreement with previously reported experimental observations and theoretical predictions. Our results establish electrostatic doping in tBG as an effective means of engineering excitonic states in adjacent semiconducting monolayers and provide a pathway toward novel optical sensor devices.

AI.tldr: This work theoretically studies how electrostatic doping of a twisted bilayer graphene (tBG) substrate reshapes the excitonic absorption spectrum of an adjacent WSe2 monolayer, revealing multiple satellite resonances arising from moiré potential coupling to exciton degrees of freedom.
AI.motivation: The paper aims to understand and engineer exciton states in a semiconducting monolayer (WSe2) placed on twisted bilayer graphene. Doping the tBG moiré superlattice creates a spatially modulated electrostatic potential that can couple to electron and hole constituents of the WSe2 exciton via screened Coulomb interaction. This offers a microscopic mechanism linking excitons to the charge-density landscape of the moiré Fermi sea, which could enable tunable optics and sensing.
AI.method: The authors perform a theoretical, microscopic study of the optical response of a WSe2 monolayer vertically stacked on tBG under electrostatic doping. They model the modulated electrostatic potential from the doped tBG moiré superlattice and its screened Coulomb coupling to the exciton electron and hole. They focus on twist angles below the magic angle (1.1 degrees), where electronic correlations are strongly enhanced, and compute excitonic absorption spectra, analyzing the interplay of exciton center-of-mass and internal degrees of freedom, as well as doping-induced hybridization between Rydberg exciton states of different orbital symmetry.
AI.result: Electrostatic doping induces pronounced modifications of the excitonic absorption spectrum, including the emergence of multiple satellite resonances. These spectral features originate from the interplay between the exciton center-of-mass and internal degrees of freedom, together with doping-induced hybridization between Rydberg exciton states of different orbital symmetry. The calculated spectra agree well with previously reported experimental observations and theoretical predictions.
AI.conclusion: Electrostatic doping in tBG is established as an effective means of engineering excitonic states in adjacent semiconducting monolayers, providing a pathway toward novel optical sensor devices.

title: Recrystallization as a tool to characterize and control the properties of cold sprayed materials: case study on 316L steel
comment: Manuscript for a submission to JTST
summary: Owing to the unique buildup mechanisms, recrystallization in cold sprayed materials significantly differs from that in conventional counterparts. In this study, the relationship between deformation-induced microstructural heterogeneity, recrystallization behavior, and mechanical properties of cold sprayed materials was investigated using EBSD and nanoindentation. The 316L stainless steel was selected as a model material. The deposit was characterized in its as-sprayed condition and after annealing at temperatures between 900 and 1100 K. Thermomechanical estimates suggest that locally, temperature can rise over 1000 K and very high dislocation densities (up to 1017 m-2) form at particle boundaries during impact, providing a strong driving force for subsequent recrystallization. The EBSD observations confirmed the intense defect accumulation and grain fragmentation localized near the particle interfaces. Recrystallization initiated preferentially in these highly strained areas after annealing at 1000 K and progressed with increasing temperature and holding time, leading to complete recrystallization after 1 h at 1100 K. The recrystallized grain-size distribution was well described by a heavy-tailed log-normal distribution, which indicates extremely heterogeneous strain partitioning generated during particle impacts. Nanoindentation measurements showed that the high hardness of the cold sprayed deposit remained largely unchanged after annealing at 900 K but gradually decreased as recrystallization progressed. We further demonstrate that controlled post-spray recrystallization can serve as a powerful tool for characterizing deformation during deposition and for tailoring the microstructure and mechanical properties of cold-sprayed materials.

AI.tldr: Recrystallization in cold sprayed 316L stainless steel originates from impact-induced heterogeneous strain and defect accumulation near particle interfaces, and post-spray annealing allows controlled tailoring of microstructure and hardness.
AI.motivation: Cold sprayed materials recrystallize via mechanisms distinct from conventional materials due to unique buildup mechanisms, yet the link between deformation-induced microstructural heterogeneity, recrystallization behavior, and mechanical properties remains unclear.
AI.method: 316L stainless steel was cold sprayed and characterized in the as-sprayed state and after annealing at 900–1100 K. Thermomechanical estimates, EBSD, and nanoindentation were used to correlate local temperature/dislocation density at particle boundaries with defect accumulation, grain fragmentation, recrystallization behavior, and hardness.
AI.result: Impact can locally raise temperature above 1000 K and generate dislocation densities up to 10^17 m^-2 at particle boundaries. EBSD confirmed intense defect accumulation and grain fragmentation near particle interfaces, where recrystallization initiated preferentially after annealing at 1000 K and completed after 1 h at 1100 K. Recrystallized grain sizes followed a heavy-tailed log-normal distribution. Hardness remained nearly unchanged after 900 K annealing and gradually decreased as recrystallization progressed.
AI.conclusion: Recrystallization preferentially initiates in highly strained particle-interface regions and progresses with temperature and holding time. Controlled post-spray recrystallization is a powerful tool for characterizing deformation during deposition and for tailoring the microstructure and mechanical properties of cold-sprayed materials.

title: Magnetic-Order-Driven Nonlinear Photocurrents in PT-Broken Antiferromagnetic MnS2 and Altermagnetic MnSe2
summary: Nonlinear photocurrent responses generally require inversion-symmetry breaking, but its origin can be magnetic rather than structural. In this study, we investigate the bulk photovoltaic effect in antiferromagnetic MnS2 and altermagnetic MnSe2, two pyrite-type semiconductors whose magnetic ordering breaks inversion symmetry P and its combination with time reversal PT, while the accompanying lattice distortion is minute. We calculate the shift current (SC) and injection current (IC) responses under linearly and circularly polarized light with and without spin-orbit coupling (SOC) and identify their symmetry-allowed tensor components using the corresponding magnetic and spin point groups, respectively. Linear SC and circular IC are symmetry-allowed in both MnS2 and MnSe2 irrespective of SOC, whereas linear IC and circular SC remain forbidden in MnS2 but become allowed in MnSe2 only when SOC is included. These results highlight the importance of SOC and the corresponding MPG analysis for a complete description of nonlinear charge photocurrents in magnetic materials. Beyond charge responses, MnSe2 supports linear shift and circular injection spin photocurrents in the nonrelativistic limit, whereas all spin-photocurrent responses are forbidden in MnS2. Our findings therefore establish inversion symmetry breaking induced by compensated magnetic order as a route to generating and controlling nonlinear photocurrents.

AI.tldr: Symmetry analysis and first-principles calculations of the bulk photovoltaic effect in antiferromagnetic MnS2 and altermagnetic MnSe2 show that magnetic-order-induced inversion-symmetry breaking enables nonlinear charge and spin photocurrents, with SOC and magnetic point-group symmetry governing which responses are allowed.
AI.motivation: Nonlinear photocurrent responses typically require inversion-symmetry breaking, which is usually assumed to be structural. The authors aim to show that this breaking can instead originate from magnetic order—specifically compensated magnetic ordering—in pyrite-type semiconductors where lattice distortion is negligible, thereby identifying a magnetic route to generating and controlling nonlinear photocurrents.
AI.method: The authors compute the shift current (SC) and injection current (IC) responses in antiferromagnetic MnS2 and altermagnetic MnSe2 under linearly and circularly polarized light, both with and without spin-orbit coupling (SOC). They determine the symmetry-allowed tensor components using the relevant magnetic and spin point groups (MPG/SPG analysis).
AI.result: Linear SC and circular IC are symmetry-allowed in both MnS2 and MnSe2 regardless of SOC. Linear IC and circular SC are forbidden in MnS2 but become allowed in MnSe2 only when SOC is included. title: Symmetry Engineering Enables Deterministic Ensemble Polarization Control in Hexagonal Boron Nitride
summary: Optical polarization is a key degree of freedom in quantum photonic and sensing technologies, enabling efficient light--matter coupling and directional emission. However, in defect ensemble-based quantum systems, orientational averaging across many defects suppresses optical anisotropy and eliminates a deterministic polarization axis. Here, symmetry engineering is introduced as a strategy to restore collective optical anisotropy in negatively charged boron vacancy (V_B^-) ensembles hosted in hexagonal boron nitride (h-BN). By imposing anisotropic in-plane tensile strain through lithographically defined nano-ridge arrays, in-plane symmetry is broken and the ensemble emission dipole is aligned with the ridge-defined strain symmetry axis. Polarization-resolved photoluminescence reveals that the polarization visibility scales with the magnitude of strain anisotropy, while the emission orientation rigidly follows the engineered symmetry axis across devices with varying strain direction. This deterministic alignment is independent of crystal orientation, establishing the optical foundation for polarization-defined ensemble spin readout and programmable photonic integration in two-dimensional quantum materials
